tricks: 'managed Oracle DR + access to OS' = RDS Custom for Oracle + cross-Region read replica

cards.q: A company wants to move its application to a serverless solution. The serverless solution needs to analyze existing and new data by using SL. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The data requires encryption and must be replicated to a different AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
cards.a: C. Load the data into the existing S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.
options: Create a new S3 bucket. Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region kays (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.

Create a new S3 bucket. Load the data into the new S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS multi-Region keys (SSE-KMS). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.

Load the data into the existing S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon Athena to query the data.

Load the data into the existing S3 bucket. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to replicate encrypted objects to an S3 bucket in another Region. Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Use Amazon RDS to query the data.
cards.explanation: LEAST operational overhead favours the existing bucket plus SSE-S3 (automatic key management) over creating a new bucket and managing SSE-KMS keys, and Athena gives serverless SQL (C). Replication of SSE-S3 objects needs no key configuration. RDS (B/D) is not serverless SQL over S3. ExamTopics majority: C.
tricks: 'serverless SQL on S3 + cross-Region encrypted replication' = Athena + SSE-KMS multi-Region keys + S3 CRR
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A company runs workloads on AWS. The company needs to connect to a service from an external provider. The service is hosted in the provider's VPC. According to the company’s security team, the connectivity must be private and must be restricted to the target service. The connection must be initiated only from the company’s VPC. Which solution will mast these requirements?
cards.a: D. Ask the provider to create a VPC endpoint for the target service. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.
options: Create a VPC peering connection between the company's VPC and the provider's VPC. Update the route table to connect to the target service.
Ask the provider to create a virtual private gateway in its VPC. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet of the company’s VPUpdate the route table to connect to the target service.
Ask the provider to create a VPC endpoint for the target service. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.
cards.explanation: AWS PrivateLink (VPC endpoint service) allows the provider to expose a service via an interface VPC endpoint that the consumer connects to from their VPC. Private, restricted to that service, initiator is the consumer. VPC peering (A) opens broad bidirectional connectivity, not restricted to one service. Virtual private gateway (B) is for VPN/Direct Connect, not service-to-service. NAT gateway (C) goes over the public Internet. Mental shortcut: 'private one-way access to a single 3rd-party service' = AWS PrivateLink.
tricks: 'private one-way access to a single 3rd-party service' = AWS PrivateLink

cards.q: A company is migrating its on-premises PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The on-premises database must remain online and accessible during the migration. The Aurora database must remain synchronized with the on-premises database. Which combination of actions must a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
cards.a: A. Create an ongoing replication task. ; C. Create an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication server.
options: Create an ongoing replication task.
Create a database backup of the on-premises database.
Create an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication server.
Convert the database schema by using the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT).
Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule to monitor the database synchronization.
cards.explanation: AWS DMS replicates data from on-prem to Aurora with minimal downtime. Set up an ongoing replication task (A) so changes keep flowing during cutover. Create a DMS replication server (C) which runs the replication. Backup (B) is a snapshot, not continuous sync. SCT (D) is needed only for heterogeneous migrations (e.g., Oracle to PostgreSQL); same-engine PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL doesn't require SCT. EventBridge monitoring (E) is observability, not the migration mechanism. Mental shortcut: 'on-prem PG to Aurora PG with continuous sync' = DMS replication server + ongoing replication task.
tricks: 'on-prem PG to Aurora PG with continuous sync' = DMS replication server + ongoing replication task

cards.q: A company uses AWS Organizations to create dedicated AWS accounts for each business unit to manage each business unit's account independently upon request. The root email recipient missed a notification that was sent to the root user email address of one account. The company wants to ensure that all future notifications are not missed. Future notifications must be limited to account administrators. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Configure all AWS account root user email addresses as distribution lists that go to a few administrators who can respond to alerts. Configure AWS account alternate contacts in the AWS Organizations console or programmatically.
options: Configure the company’s email server to forward notification email messages that are sent to the AWS account root user email address to all users in the organization.

Configure all AWS account root user email addresses as distribution lists that go to a few administrators who can respond to alerts. Configure AWS account alternate contacts in the AWS Organizations console or programmatically.
Configure all AWS account root user email messages to be sent to one administrator who is responsible for monitoring alerts and forwarding those alerts to the appropriate groups.

Configure all existing AWS accounts and all newly created accounts to use the same root user email address. Configure AWS account alternate contacts in the AWS Organizations console or programmatically.
cards.explanation: Use distribution lists (group emails) for root user emails so multiple admins receive notifications, and configure the alternate contacts (Billing, Operations, Security) in Organizations so the right team gets domain-specific notifications. Forward all emails to everyone (A) is noisy. Single admin (C) repeats the original failure mode. Same root email for all accounts (D) violates AWS account isolation guidance. Mental shortcut: 'never miss AWS account notifications' = distribution lists + alternate contacts.
tricks: 'never miss AWS account notifications' = distribution lists + alternate contacts
'block root user actions in member accounts' = SCP at Organizations level (only thing that constrains root)

cards.q: A company runs its ecommerce application on AWS. Every new order is published as a massage in a RabbitMQ queue that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a single Availability Zone. These messages are processed by a different application that runs on a separate EC2 instance. This application stores the details in a PostgreSQL database on another EC2 instance. All the EC2 instances are in the same Availability Zone. The company needs to redesign its architecture to provide the highest availability with the least operational overhead. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.
options: Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database.

Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application. Create a third Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database
cards.explanation: Amazon MQ active/standby (HA RabbitMQ-compatible managed service) + ASG for application across AZs + RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ. All managed services, all Multi-AZ. Self-managed RabbitMQ on EC2 ASG (C, D) loses the broker pattern (RabbitMQ doesn't auto-replicate state across instances in an ASG). PostgreSQL on EC2 ASG (A, D) is wrong, you can't put a stateful single-master DB behind an ASG. Mental shortcut: 'highest availability for RabbitMQ + app + PostgreSQL with LEAST ops' = Amazon MQ + ASG app + RDS Multi-AZ.
tricks: 'highest availability for RabbitMQ + app + PostgreSQL with LEAST ops' = Amazon MQ + ASG app + RDS Multi-AZ
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A reporting team receives files each day in an Amazon S3 bucket. The reporting team manually reviews and copies the files from this initial S3 bucket to an analysis S3 bucket each day at the same time to use with Amazon QuickSight. Additional teams are starting to send more files in larger sizes to the initial S3 bucket. The reporting team wants to move the files automatically analysis S3 bucket as the files enter the initial S3 bucket. The reporting team also wants to use AWS Lambda functions to run pattern-matching code on the copied data. In addition, the reporting team wants to send the data files to a pipeline in Amazon SageMaker Pipelines. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
cards.a: D. Configure S3 replication between the S3 buckets. Configure the analysis S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events). Configure an ObjectCreated rule in EventBridge (CloudWatch Events). Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets for the rule.
options: Create a Lambda function to copy the files to the analysis S3 bucket. Create an S3 event notification for the analysis S3 bucket. Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as destinations of the event notification. Configure s3:ObjectCreated:Put as the event type.

Create a Lambda function to copy the files to the analysis S3 bucket. Configure the analysis S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events). Configure an ObjectCreated rule in EventBridge (CloudWatch Events). Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets for the rule.

Configure S3 replication between the S3 buckets. Create an S3 event notification for the analysis S3 bucket. Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as destinations of the event notification. Configure s3:ObjectCreated:Put as the event type.

Configure S3 replication between the S3 buckets. Configure the analysis S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events). Configure an ObjectCreated rule in EventBridge (CloudWatch Events). Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets for the rule.
cards.explanation: S3 Replication moves files automatically without Lambda. Then EventBridge handles object-created events with multiple targets, both Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines, in a single rule. Native multi-target. S3 event notifications (A, C) support fewer destinations and less flexibility than EventBridge. Lambda copying files (A, B) is custom code where S3 Replication does the same natively. Mental shortcut: 'auto-copy + multi-target on object created + LEAST ops' = S3 Replication + EventBridge with multiple targets.
tricks: 'auto-copy + multi-target on object created + LEAST ops' = S3 Replication + EventBridge with multiple targets
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A solutions architect needs to help a company optimize the cost of running an application on AWS. The application will use Amazon EC2 instances, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda for compute within the architecture. The EC2 instances will run the data ingestion layer of the application. EC2 usage will be sporadic and unpredictable. Workloads that run on EC2 instances can be interrupted at any time. The application front end will run on Fargate, and Lambda will serve the API layer. The front-end utilization and API layer utilization will be predictable over the course of the next year. Which combination of purchasing options will provide the MOST cost-effective solution for hosting this application? (Choose two.)
cards.a: A. Use Spot Instances for the data ingestion layer ; C. Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.
options: Use Spot Instances for the data ingestion layer
Use On-Demand Instances for the data ingestion layer
Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.
Purchase 1-year All Upfront Reserved instances for the data ingestion layer.
Purchase a 1-year EC2 instance Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.
cards.explanation: Sporadic + interruptible EC2 ingestion = Spot (A), max savings, fits the workload. Predictable Fargate + Lambda for a year = Compute Savings Plan (C), which covers EC2, Fargate, AND Lambda flexibly with up to 66% off. EC2 Instance Savings Plan (E) only covers EC2, doesn't cover Fargate/Lambda. Reserved Instances (D) is for steady EC2 use, doesn't apply to interruptible ingestion. On-Demand (B) is most expensive for sporadic. Mental shortcut: 'interruptible + predictable Fargate/Lambda' = Spot + Compute Savings Plan.
tricks: 'interruptible + predictable Fargate/Lambda' = Spot + Compute Savings Plan
'containers without managing servers' = ECS/EKS on AWS Fargate

cards.q: A company runs a web-based portal that provides users with global breaking news, local alerts, and weather updates. The portal delivers each user a personalized view by using mixture of static and dynamic content. Content is served over HTTPS through an API server running on an Amazon EC2 instance behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company wants the portal to provide this content to its users across the world as quickly as possible. How should a solutions architect design the application to ensure the LEAST amount of latency for all users?
cards.a: A. Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve all static and dynamic content by specifying the ALB as an origin.
options: Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve all static and dynamic content by specifying the ALB as an origin.
Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.
Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the static content. Serve the dynamic content directly from the ALB.
Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.
cards.explanation: CloudFront in front of an ALB with a single Region serves both static (cached) and dynamic (cache-bypass with edge optimization for TLS, TCP, route over backbone) globally with the lowest latency. CloudFront accelerates dynamic via edge optimizations even when not cached. Two Regions (B, D) is heavy ops vs one CloudFront. Static-only CloudFront with dynamic direct ALB (C) keeps dynamic on a single far-Region path. Mental shortcut: 'global static + dynamic + LEAST latency' = CloudFront in front of ALB.
tricks: 'global static + dynamic + LEAST latency' = CloudFront in front of ALB

cards.q: A gaming company is designing a highly available architecture. The application runs on a modified Linux kernel and supports only UDP-based traffic. The company needs the front-end tier to provide the best possible user experience. That tier must have low latency, route traffic to the nearest edge location, and provide static IP addresses for entry into the application endpoints. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
cards.a: C. Configure AWS Global Accelerator to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group.
options: Configure Amazon Route 53 to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in AWS Application Auto Scaling.
Configure Amazon CloudFront to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in an AWS Application Auto Scaling group.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group.
Configure Amazon API Gateway to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group.
cards.explanation: Modified Linux kernel + UDP = EC2 (Lambda and Fargate can't run modified kernels). UDP + lowest latency + static IPs + edge routing = Global Accelerator. NLB to forward UDP to EC2 ASG. CloudFront (B) is HTTP/S only. ALB (A, D) doesn't support UDP. Mental shortcut: 'UDP + static IPs + low-latency edge entry + EC2 backend' = Global Accelerator + NLB + EC2.
tricks: 'UDP + static IPs + low-latency edge entry + EC2 backend' = Global Accelerator + NLB + EC2
'UDP traffic' = NLB only (ALB does NOT support UDP); for global VoIP add Global Accelerator

cards.q: A company wants to migrate its existing on-premises monolithic application to AWS. The company wants to keep as much of the front-end code and the backend code as possible. However, the company wants to break the application into smaller applications. A different team will manage each application. The company needs a highly scalable solution that minimizes operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: D. Host the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Set up an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS as the target.
options: Host the application on AWS Lambda. Integrate the application with Amazon API Gateway.
Host the application with AWS Amplify. Connect the application to an Amazon API Gateway API that is integrated with AWS Lambda.
Host the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Set up an Application Load Balancer with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group as targets.
Host the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Set up an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS as the target.
cards.explanation: Containerizing the monolith and breaking it into smaller services on ECS with ALB target groups lets each team own a service while keeping most of the existing code (lift-and-shift to containers). Lambda (A) requires significant code changes. Amplify (B) is for front-end hosting, not containers. EC2 + ASG + ALB (C) keeps OS-level operational overhead. Mental shortcut: 'split monolith into multiple services + reuse code + LEAST ops' = ECS + ALB.
tricks: 'split monolith into multiple services + reuse code + LEAST ops' = ECS + ALB

cards.q: A company recently started using Amazon Aurora as the data store for its global ecommerce application. When large reports are run, developers report that the ecommerce application is performing poorly. After reviewing metrics in Amazon CloudWatch, a solutions architect finds that the ReadIOPS and CPUUtilizalion metrics are spiking when monthly reports run. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?
cards.a: B. Migrate the monthly reporting to an Aurora Replica.
options: Migrate the monthly reporting to Amazon Redshift.
Migrate the monthly reporting to an Aurora Replica.
Migrate the Aurora database to a larger instance class.
Increase the Provisioned IOPS on the Aurora instance.
cards.explanation: Spiking ReadIOPS + CPU during reports = read-heavy reporting workload. Aurora Replicas offload reads with no extra storage cost (Aurora storage is shared between writer and replicas), most cost-effective. Redshift (A) requires data migration and is overkill. Larger instance class (C) doubles cost. Provisioned IOPS (D) doesn't apply to Aurora (it has its own auto-scaling storage). Mental shortcut: 'read-heavy reporting on Aurora + cheapest' = Aurora Replica.
tricks: 'read-heavy reporting on Aurora + cheapest' = Aurora Replica

cards.q: A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics software is written in PHP and uses a MySQL database. The analytics software, the web server that provides PHP, and the database server are all hosted on the EC2 instance. The application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: D. Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group with the launch template Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.
options: Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load to each EC2 instance.

Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.

Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization surpasses 75%.

Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group with the launch template Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.
cards.explanation: Move DB to Aurora MySQL (managed). AMI of web app + launch template + Auto Scaling group on Spot Fleet (cheapest stateless compute) + ALB. Truly scales seamlessly with the cheapest compute. Two static EC2 + ALB (A) doesn't scale. Two static EC2 + Route 53 (B) is even worse. Lambda resize (C) is reactive vertical scaling, not horizontal. Mental shortcut: 'scale seamlessly + cheapest stateless web' = ASG with Spot Fleet + ALB + Aurora.
tricks: 'scale seamlessly + cheapest stateless web' = ASG with Spot Fleet + ALB + Aurora

cards.q: A company runs a stateless web application in production on a group of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application experiences heavy usage during an 8-hour period each business day. Application usage is moderate and steady overnight. Application usage is low during weekends. The company wants to minimize its EC2 costs without affecting the availability of the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Use Reserved Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.
options: Use Spot Instances for the entire workload.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.
Use On-Demand Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot Instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.
Use Dedicated Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use On-Demand Instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.
cards.explanation: Steady baseline (overnight + weekend usage) = Reserved Instances for predictable cost savings. Burst capacity during 8h peak = Spot Instances (cheapest, ASG can mix). Combining RI baseline + Spot burst is the textbook 'minimize EC2 cost with predictable + burst' pattern. On-Demand baseline (C) is more expensive than RI for steady use. Pure Spot (A) risks the baseline being interrupted. Dedicated (D) is far more expensive. Mental shortcut: 'predictable baseline + variable burst' = Reserved + Spot.
tricks: 'predictable baseline + variable burst' = Reserved + Spot

cards.q: A company needs to retain application log files for a critical application for 10 years. The application team regularly accesses logs from the past month for troubleshooting, but logs older than 1 month are rarely accessed. The application generates more than 10 TB of logs per month. Which storage option meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: B. Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options: Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
cards.explanation: S3 + S3 Lifecycle to Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest 10-year retention pattern for log files at 10TB/month. AWS Backup for S3 transitions (A) doesn't apply, S3 lifecycle is the native mechanism. CloudWatch Logs (C, D) is more expensive than S3 for long-term storage and isn't designed for 10-year retention at TB scale. AWS Backup or S3 Lifecycle for CloudWatch Logs (C, D) doesn't archive CW Logs to Glacier. Mental shortcut: 'large log retention years + cheapest' = export to S3 + Lifecycle to Deep Archive.
tricks: 'large log retention years + cheapest' = export to S3 + Lifecycle to Deep Archive

cards.q: A company has a data ingestion workflow that includes the following components: An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that receives notifications about new data deliveries An AWS Lambda function that processes and stores the data The ingestion workflow occasionally fails because of network connectivity issues. When failure occurs, the corresponding data is not ingested unless the company manually reruns the job. What should a solutions architect do to ensure that all notifications are eventually processed?
cards.a: D. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as the on-failure destination. Modify the Lambda function to process messages in the queue.
options: Configure the Lambda function for deployment across multiple Availability Zones.
Modify the Lambda function's configuration to increase the CPU and memory allocations for the function.
Configure the SNS topic’s retry strategy to increase both the number of retries and the wait time between retries.
Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as the on-failure destination. Modify the Lambda function to process messages in the queue.
cards.explanation: Lambda destinations: configure SQS as the on-failure destination so failed Lambda invocations land in a queue automatically; the Lambda (or another consumer) processes them later. Multi-AZ Lambda (A) is automatic, doesn't help with retries. CPU/memory (B) doesn't fix transient failures. SNS retry strategy (C) is limited to ~3 retries over 1 hour, not enough for connectivity issues. Mental shortcut: 'never lose Lambda invocations on transient failure' = Lambda on-failure destination = SQS.
tricks: 'never lose Lambda invocations on transient failure' = Lambda on-failure destination = SQS

cards.q: A company has a service that produces event data. The company wants to use AWS to process the event data as it is received. The data is written in a specific order that must be maintained throughout processing. The company wants to implement a solution that minimizes operational overhead. How should a solutions architect accomplish this?
cards.a: A. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue.
options: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an AWS Lambda function as a subscriber.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to hold messages. Set up an AWS Lambda function to process messages from the queue independently.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to deliver notifications containing payloads to process. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a subscriber.
cards.explanation: SQS FIFO preserves message order (first-in-first-out per message group) and integrates natively with Lambda. SNS standard (B) and SQS standard (C) don't preserve order. SNS to SQS (D) doesn't preserve order on the SNS hop. Mental shortcut: 'process in order + LEAST ops' = SQS FIFO + Lambda.
tricks: 'process in order + LEAST ops' = SQS FIFO + Lambda

cards.q: A company is migrating an application from on-premises servers to Amazon EC2 instances. As part of the migration design requirements, a solutions architect must implement infrastructure metric alarms. The company does not need to take action if CPU utilization increases to more than 50% for a short burst of time. However, if the CPU utilization increases to more than 50% and read IOPS on the disk are high at the same time, the company needs to act as soon as possible. The solutions architect also must reduce false alarms. What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
cards.a: A. Create Amazon CloudWatch composite alarms where possible.
options: Create Amazon CloudWatch composite alarms where possible.
Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize the metrics and react to issues quickly.
Create Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries to monitor the application and raise an alarm.
Create single Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms with multiple metric thresholds where possible.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch composite alarms combine multiple metric alarms with AND/OR logic so you only fire when both CPU>50% AND ReadIOPS high are true at once, reducing false positives. Dashboards (B) are visualization, not alerting. Synthetics (C) is web monitoring. Single metric alarms with multiple thresholds (D) don't exist; alarms have one threshold per metric. Mental shortcut: 'fire alarm only when multiple conditions are true at once' = CloudWatch composite alarm.
tricks: 'fire alarm only when multiple conditions are true at once' = CloudWatch composite alarm

cards.q: A company wants to migrate its on-premises data center to AWS. According to the company's compliance requirements, the company can use only the ap-northeast-3 Region. Company administrators are not permitted to connect VPCs to the internet. Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
cards.a: A. Use AWS Control Tower to implement data residency guardrails to deny internet access and deny access to all AWS Regions except ap- northeast-3. ; C. Use AWS Organizations to configure service control policies (SCPS) that prevent VPCs from gaining internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3.
options: Use AWS Control Tower to implement data residency guardrails to deny internet access and deny access to all AWS Regions except ap- northeast-3.
Use rules in AWS WAF to prevent internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3 in the AWS account settings.
Use AWS Organizations to configure service control policies (SCPS) that prevent VPCs from gaining internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3.
Create an outbound rule for the network ACL in each VPC to deny all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0. Create an IAM policy for each user to prevent the use of any AWS Region other than ap-northeast-3.
Use AWS Config to activate managed rules to detect and alert for internet gateways and to detect and alert for new resources deployed outside of ap-northeast-3.
cards.explanation: Control Tower data residency guardrails (A) provide pre-built controls that deny Internet access AND deny non-allowed Regions in one product. SCPs in Organizations (C) achieve the same enforcement at the org level via service control policies. WAF (B) is for web request filtering, not VPC Internet access or Region restriction. NACL deny + per-user IAM (D) is brittle and per-user IAM is unmanageable. Config rules (E) only detect, don't prevent. Mental shortcut: 'enforce no Internet + only one Region across an org' = Control Tower guardrails OR SCPs.
tricks: 'enforce no Internet + only one Region across an org' = Control Tower guardrails OR SCPs

cards.q: A company uses a three-tier web application to provide training to new employees. The application is accessed for only 12 hours every day. The company is using an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance to store information and wants to minimize costs. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
cards.a: D. Create AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance. Create Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules to invoke the Lambda functions. Configure the Lambda functions as event targets for the rules.
options: Configure an IAM policy for AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Create an IAM role for the policy. Update the trust relationship of the role. Set up automatic start and stop for the DB instance.

Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache cluster that gives users the ability to access the data from the cache when the DB instance is stopped. Invalidate the cache after the DB instance is started.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Create an IAM role that grants access to Amazon RDS. Attach the role to the EC2 instance. Configure a cron job to start and stop the EC2 instance on the desired schedule.

Create AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance. Create Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules to invoke the Lambda functions. Configure the Lambda functions as event targets for the rules.
cards.explanation: Schedule start/stop of the RDS instance via EventBridge cron rules invoking Lambda functions. RDS DB instance can be stopped up to 7 days at a time so daily 12h-off works. ElastiCache (B) is unrelated. EC2 cron (C) requires running an EC2 just to manage RDS. SSM Session Manager (A) is for shell access, doesn't schedule RDS start/stop. Mental shortcut: 'cost-optimize RDS used part of the day' = EventBridge schedule + Lambda start/stop.
tricks: 'cost-optimize RDS used part of the day' = EventBridge schedule + Lambda start/stop

cards.q: A company sells ringtones created from clips of popular songs. The files containing the ringtones are stored in Amazon S3 Standard and are at least 128 KB in size. The company has millions of files, but downloads are infrequent for ringtones older than 90 days. The company needs to save money on storage while keeping the most accessed files readily available for its users. Which action should the company take to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: D. Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.
options: Configure S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage for the initial storage tier of the objects.
Move the files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and configure it to move objects to a less expensive storage tier after 90 days.
Configure S3 inventory to manage objects and move them to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.
Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.
cards.explanation: Files >128KB accessed initially then rarely after 90 days = Lifecycle to Standard-IA after 90 days. Standard-IA min size is 128KB so the files qualify. Standard-IA initial (A) is wrong, files are accessed often initially. Intelligent-Tiering (B) costs more than Lifecycle for clearly known patterns and adds monitoring fees. S3 Inventory (C) is a metadata report, not a tier transition. Mental shortcut: 'known access pattern + after N days infrequent' = Lifecycle to Standard-IA at the cutoff.
tricks: 'known access pattern + after N days infrequent' = Lifecycle to Standard-IA at the cutoff

cards.q: A company needs to save the results from a medical trial to an Amazon S3 repository. The repository must allow a few scientists to add new files and must restrict all other users to read-only access. No users can have the ability to modify or delete any files in the repository. The company must keep every file in the repository for a minimum of 1 year after its creation date. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 365 days.
options: Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a legal hold of 1 year.
Use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 365 days.
Use an IAM role to restrict all users from deleting or changing objects in the S3 bucket. Use an S3 bucket policy to only allow the IAM role.

Configure the S3 bucket to invoke an AWS Lambda function every time an object is added. Configure the function to track the hash of the saved object so that modified objects can be marked accordingly.
cards.explanation: Object Lock Compliance mode with 365-day retention prevents anyone (including root) from deleting or modifying objects until retention expires. Bucket policy controls write access. Governance + legal hold (A) can be bypassed by a privileged user. IAM-only restriction (C) can be circumvented by anyone with root. Lambda hash tracking (D) is detective, not preventive. Mental shortcut: '1-year minimum + no one can delete or modify' = Object Lock Compliance mode + retention period.
tricks: '1-year minimum + no one can delete or modify' = Object Lock Compliance mode + retention period

cards.q: A large media company hosts a web application on AWS. The company wants to start caching confidential media files so that users around the world will have reliable access to the files. The content is stored in Amazon S3 buckets. The company must deliver the content quickly, regardless of where the requests originate geographically. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: C. Deploy Amazon CloudFront to connect the S3 buckets to CloudFront edge servers.
options: Use AWS DataSync to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.
Deploy AWS Global Accelerator to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.
Deploy Amazon CloudFront to connect the S3 buckets to CloudFront edge servers.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.
cards.explanation: CloudFront caches S3 content at hundreds of edge locations globally for fast access regardless of user location. DataSync (A) transfers data, doesn't cache. Global Accelerator (B) is for TCP/UDP routing, not HTTP caching of static files. SQS (D) is messaging. Mental shortcut: 'cache S3 content globally + reliable + fast' = CloudFront.
tricks: 'cache S3 content globally + reliable + fast' = CloudFront

cards.q: A company produces batch data that comes from different databases. The company also produces live stream data from network sensors and application APIs. The company needs to consolidate all the data into one place for business analytics. The company needs to process the incoming data and then stage the data in different Amazon S3 buckets. Teams will later run one-time queries and import the data into a business intelligence tool to show key performance indicators (KPIs). Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
cards.a: A. Use Amazon Athena for one-time queries. Use Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for KPIs. ; E. Use blueprints in AWS Lake Formation to identify the data that can be ingested into a data lake. Use AWS Glue to crawl the source, extract the data, and load the data into Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format.
options: Use Amazon Athena for one-time queries. Use Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for KPIs.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for one-time queries. Use Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for KPIs.
Create custom AWS Lambda functions to move the individual records from the databases to an Amazon Redshift cluster.
Use an AWS Glue extract, transform, and load (ETL) job to convert the data into JSON format. Load the data into multiple Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) clusters.

Use blueprints in AWS Lake Formation to identify the data that can be ingested into a data lake. Use AWS Glue to crawl the source, extract the data, and load the data into Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format.
cards.explanation: Lake Formation blueprint + Glue (E) sets up the data lake ingestion automatically including transformation to Parquet. Athena (A) queries the lake with SQL on demand and QuickSight builds KPI dashboards on top. Kinesis Data Analytics (B) is for streaming SQL, not one-time queries. Custom Lambda (C) is high overhead. OpenSearch (D) is for search, not BI/lake. Mental shortcut: 'data lake + one-time queries + KPI dashboards + LEAST ops' = Lake Formation + Glue + Athena + QuickSight.
tricks: 'data lake + one-time queries + KPI dashboards + LEAST ops' = Lake Formation + Glue + Athena + QuickSight
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A company stores data in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster. The company must store all the data for 5 years and must delete all the data after 5 years. The company also must indefinitely keep audit logs of actions that are performed within the database. Currently, the company has automated backups configured for Aurora. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
cards.a: D. Configure an Amazon CloudWatch Logs export for the DB cluster. ; E. Use AWS Backup to take the backups and to keep the backups for 5 years.
options: Take a manual snapshot of the DB cluster.
Create a lifecycle policy for the automated backups.
Configure automated backup retention for 5 years.
Configure an Amazon CloudWatch Logs export for the DB cluster.
Use AWS Backup to take the backups and to keep the backups for 5 years.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup (E) for the 5-year DB cluster retention, native managed service for Aurora. CloudWatch Logs export (D) for indefinite audit log retention by exporting to a CW Logs group with retention set to never expire. Manual snapshot (A) doesn't satisfy ongoing 5-year retention. Lifecycle policy on automated backups (B) doesn't extend retention beyond max. Aurora automated backup max retention is 35 days, can't reach 5 years (C). Mental shortcut: 'long Aurora backups + indefinite audit logs' = AWS Backup + CloudWatch Logs export.
tricks: 'long Aurora backups + indefinite audit logs' = AWS Backup + CloudWatch Logs export

cards.q: A solutions architect is optimizing a website for an upcoming musical event. Videos of the performances will be streamed in real time and then will be available on demand. The event is expected to attract a global online audience. Which service will improve the performance of both the real-time and on-demand streaming?
cards.a: A. Amazon CloudFront
options: Amazon CloudFront
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon Route 53
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
cards.explanation: CloudFront supports both real-time streaming (HTTP-based via segments like HLS/DASH) and on-demand video, with global edge caching. Global Accelerator (B) is for TCP/UDP routing, not video segment caching. Route 53 (C) is DNS. S3 Transfer Acceleration (D) is for upload to S3, not viewer streaming. Mental shortcut: 'global video streaming + real-time + on-demand' = CloudFront.
tricks: 'global video streaming + real-time + on-demand' = CloudFront

cards.q: A company is running a publicly accessible serverless application that uses Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The application’s traffic recently spiked due to fraudulent requests from botnets. Which steps should a solutions architect take to block requests from unauthorized users? (Choose two.)
cards.a: A. Create a usage plan with an API key that is shared with genuine users only. ; C. Implement an AWS WAF rule to target malicious requests and trigger actions to filter them out.
options: Create a usage plan with an API key that is shared with genuine users only.
Integrate logic within the Lambda function to ignore the requests from fraudulent IP addresses.
Implement an AWS WAF rule to target malicious requests and trigger actions to filter them out.
Convert the existing public API to a private API. Update the DNS records to redirect users to the new API endpoint.
Create an IAM role for each user attempting to access the API. A user will assume the role when making the API call.
cards.explanation: WAF rules (C) on the API Gateway block malicious requests, including bot patterns, geo, rate limits. API Gateway usage plan with API keys (A) limits the API to authenticated genuine users so botnets without keys are rejected. Lambda IP filtering (B) wastes compute on the rejected requests. Private API (D) breaks public access. Per-user IAM roles (E) is unscalable for public APIs. Mental shortcut: 'block bots on public API' = WAF + usage plan with API keys.
tricks: 'block bots on public API' = WAF + usage plan with API keys
'Lambda overwhelmed by spikes' = put SQS in front for buffering

cards.q: An ecommerce company hosts its analytics application in the AWS Cloud. The application generates about 300 MB of data each month. The data is stored in JSON format. The company is evaluating a disaster recovery solution to back up the data. The data must be accessible in milliseconds if it is needed, and the data must be kept for 30 days. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: C. Amazon S3 Standard
options: Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service)
Amazon S3 Glacier
Amazon S3 Standard
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
cards.explanation: 300 MB/month + ms access for DR + 30-day retention = S3 Standard, cheapest for small volume + always-immediate access. OpenSearch (A) is for search, expensive cluster. Glacier (B) has retrieval delays. RDS (D) requires running a database 24/7. Mental shortcut: 'small data + ms access + cheap' = S3 Standard.
tricks: 'small data + ms access + cheap' = S3 Standard

cards.q: A company has a small Python application that processes JSON documents and outputs the results to an on-premises SQL database. The application runs thousands of times each day. The company wants to move the application to the AWS Cloud. The company needs a highly available solution that maximizes scalability and minimizes operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Place the JSON documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an AWS Lambda function that runs the Python code to process the documents as they arrive in the S3 bucket. Store the results in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.
options: Place the JSON documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Run the Python code on multiple Amazon EC2 instances to process the documents. Store the results in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.

Place the JSON documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an AWS Lambda function that runs the Python code to process the documents as they arrive in the S3 bucket. Store the results in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.

Place the JSON documents in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Use the EBS Multi-Attach feature to attach the volume to multiple Amazon EC2 instances. Run the Python code on the EC2 instances to process the documents. Store the results on an Amazon RDS DB instance.

Place the JSON documents in an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as messages. Deploy the Python code as a container on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster that is configured with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Use the container to process the SQS messages. Store the results on an Amazon RDS DB instance.
cards.explanation: S3 + Lambda (event-driven on S3 PUT) + Aurora is fully serverless: highly available, scales automatically, no servers to manage. EC2-based options (A) require capacity planning. EBS Multi-Attach (C) is for shared block storage between same-AZ EC2, not workflow orchestration. SQS + ECS on EC2 (D) keeps EC2 management overhead. Mental shortcut: 'event-driven JSON processing + LEAST ops + scale' = S3 + Lambda + Aurora.
tricks: 'event-driven JSON processing + LEAST ops + scale' = S3 + Lambda + Aurora

cards.q: A company wants to use high performance computing (HPC) infrastructure on AWS for financial risk modeling. The company’s HPC workloads run on Linux. Each HPC workflow runs on hundreds of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, is short-lived, and generates thousands of output files that are ultimately stored in persistent storage for analytics and long-term future use. The company seeks a cloud storage solution that permits the copying of on-premises data to long-term persistent storage to make data available for processing by all EC2 instances. The solution should also be a high performance file system that is integrated with persistent storage to read and write datasets and output files. Which combination of AWS services meets these requirements?
cards.a: A. Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with Amazon S3
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon S3 Glacier integrated with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon S3 bucket with a VPC endpoint integrated with an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume
cards.explanation: FSx for Lustre is the AWS managed Lustre file system designed exactly for HPC. It integrates natively with S3, presenting S3 objects as files in the FSx file system and writing back to S3 for persistence. FSx for Windows (B) is SMB Windows, wrong protocol. S3 Glacier + EBS (C) is archive + block storage, not a parallel file system. S3 + EBS gp2 (D) doesn't integrate with HPC compute. Mental shortcut: 'HPC + parallel file system + integrated with S3' = FSx for Lustre + S3.
tricks: 'HPC + parallel file system + integrated with S3' = FSx for Lustre + S3
'fault-tolerant + cheapest' = Spot Instances (up to 90% off, 2-min interruption notice)

cards.q: A company is building a containerized application on premises and decides to move the application to AWS. The application will have thousands of users soon after it is deployed. The company is unsure how to manage the deployment of containers at scale. The company needs to deploy the containerized application in a highly available architecture that minimizes operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: A. Store container images in an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type to run the containers. Use target tracking to scale automatically based on demand.
options: Store container images in an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type to run the containers. Use target tracking to scale automatically based on demand.

Store container images in an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Amazon EC2 launch type to run the containers. Use target tracking to scale automatically based on demand.

Store container images in a repository that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. Run the containers on EC2 instances that are spread across multiple Availability Zones. Monitor the average CPU utilization in Amazon CloudWatch. Launch new EC2 instances as needed.

Create an Amazon EC2 Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that contains the container image. Launch EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to scale out EC2 instances when the average CPU utilization threshold is breached.
cards.explanation: ECR for images + ECS on Fargate for serverless containers + target tracking auto scaling = highest scalability with no node management. ECR + ECS on EC2 (B) requires managing EC2 worker nodes. Self-hosted registry (C) is high ops. AMI baked container (D) defeats the purpose of containers and adds AMI rebuild cycles. Mental shortcut: 'containers at scale + LEAST ops' = ECR + ECS on Fargate + target tracking.
tricks: 'containers at scale + LEAST ops' = ECR + ECS on Fargate + target tracking

cards.q: A company has two applications: a sender application that sends messages with payloads to be processed and a processing application intended to receive the messages with payloads. The company wants to implement an AWS service to handle messages between the two applications. The sender application can send about 1,000 messages each hour. The messages may take up to 2 days to be processed: If the messages fail to process, they must be retained so that they do not impact the processing of any remaining messages. Which solution meets these requirements and is the MOST operationally efficient?
cards.a: C. Integrate the sender and processor applications with an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure a dead-letter queue to collect the messages that failed to process.
options: Set up an Amazon EC2 instance running a Redis database. Configure both applications to use the instance. Store, process, and delete the messages, respectively.
Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream to receive the messages from the sender application. Integrate the processing application with the Kinesis Client Library (KCL).
Integrate the sender and processor applications with an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure a dead-letter queue to collect the messages that failed to process.
Subscribe the processing application to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to receive notifications to process. Integrate the sender application to write to the SNS topic.
cards.explanation: SQS retains messages up to 14 days (and processing window of 2 days fits), supports DLQ for failed messages so they don't impede the queue. Producer rate of 1000/h is well within SQS limits. Redis EC2 (A) is high ops and not durable storage by default. Kinesis Data Streams (B) is overkill for 1000 msg/h and has 24h default retention (extendable to 365 days but more complex). SNS (D) doesn't store messages, no DLQ semantics for SNS->subscriber for 2-day delay. Mental shortcut: 'queue + retain failed messages + 2-day processing window' = SQS + DLQ.
tricks: 'queue + retain failed messages + 2-day processing window' = SQS + DLQ

cards.q: A solutions architect must design a solution that uses Amazon CloudFront with an Amazon S3 origin to store a static website. The company’s security policy requires that all website traffic be inspected by AWS WAF. How should the solutions architect comply with these requirements?
cards.a: D. Configure Amazon CloudFront and Amazon S3 to use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict access to the S3 bucket. Enable AWS WAF on the distribution.
options: Configure an S3 bucket policy to accept requests coming from the AWS WAF Amazon Resource Name (ARN) only.
Configure Amazon CloudFront to forward all incoming requests to AWS WAF before requesting content from the S3 origin.
Configure a security group that allows Amazon CloudFront IP addresses to access Amazon S3 only. Associate AWS WAF to CloudFront.
Configure Amazon CloudFront and Amazon S3 to use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict access to the S3 bucket. Enable AWS WAF on the distribution.
cards.explanation: OAI (or OAC) restricts S3 access to CloudFront only. WAF associated with the CloudFront distribution inspects all incoming traffic before it reaches CloudFront/S3. Bucket policy with WAF ARN (A) doesn't make sense, WAF doesn't have an executing principal. Forwarding requests through WAF first (B) misunderstands the architecture, WAF attaches to CloudFront. Security group with CloudFront IPs (C) doesn't apply to S3. Mental shortcut: 'CloudFront + S3 + WAF inspection' = OAI/OAC + WAF on CloudFront.
tricks: 'CloudFront + S3 + WAF inspection' = OAI/OAC + WAF on CloudFront
'reduce latency for global users' = CloudFront edge caching

cards.q: Organizers for a global event want to put daily reports online as static HTML pages. The pages are expected to generate millions of views from users around the world. The files are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. A solutions architect has been asked to design an efficient and effective solution. Which action should the solutions architect take to accomplish this?
cards.a: D. Use Amazon CloudFront with the S3 bucket as its origin.
options: Generate presigned URLs for the files.
Use cross-Region replication to all Regions.
Use the geoproximity feature of Amazon Route 53.
Use Amazon CloudFront with the S3 bucket as its origin.
cards.explanation: CloudFront with S3 origin caches static HTML at edge globally for low latency at millions of users. Presigned URLs (A) authorize specific users, not for public broadcast. Cross-Region replication (B) increases storage costs and doesn't accelerate user access. Geoproximity routing (C) without CloudFront still hits the single S3 bucket from far away. Mental shortcut: 'static content + millions of global views' = CloudFront + S3.
tricks: 'static content + millions of global views' = CloudFront + S3

cards.q: A company runs a production application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads the data from an Amazon SQS queue and processes the messages in parallel. The message volume is unpredictable and often has intermittent traffic. This application should continually process messages without any downtime. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: C. Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use Spot Instances to handle additional capacity.
options: Use Spot Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required.
Use Reserved Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use Spot Instances to handle additional capacity.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use On-Demand Instances to handle additional capacity.
cards.explanation: Continuous baseline + intermittent spikes + cheapest with no downtime = Reserved for the always-on baseline, Spot for the burst portion. Pure Spot (A) risks downtime when capacity is reclaimed. Pure Reserved (B) wastes RIs sized for max capacity. Reserved + On-Demand (D) is more expensive than Reserved + Spot. Mental shortcut: 'continuous + intermittent burst + cheapest, never down' = Reserved baseline + Spot burst.
tricks: 'continuous + intermittent burst + cheapest, never down' = Reserved baseline + Spot burst

cards.q: A security team wants to limit access to specific services or actions in all of the team’s AWS accounts. All accounts belong to a large organization in AWS Organizations. The solution must be scalable and there must be a single point where permissions can be maintained. What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this?
cards.a: D. Create a service control policy in the root organizational unit to deny access to the services or actions.
options: Create an ACL to provide access to the services or actions.
Create a security group to allow accounts and attach it to user groups.
Create cross-account roles in each account to deny access to the services or actions.
Create a service control policy in the root organizational unit to deny access to the services or actions.
cards.explanation: Service Control Policies on the root OU enforce permission boundaries across every account in the organization from a single place, exactly the requested 'single point + scalable + limit access'. ACL (A) doesn't apply to AWS services. Security groups (B) are network controls, not IAM permissions. Cross-account roles (C) require per-account configuration, doesn't scale. Mental shortcut: 'limit specific services across all accounts in an Organization' = SCP.
tricks: 'limit specific services across all accounts in an Organization' = SCP

cards.q: A company is concerned about the security of its public web application due to recent web attacks. The application uses an Application Load Balancer (ALB). A solutions architect must reduce the risk of DDoS attacks against the application. What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
cards.a: C. Enable AWS Shield Advanced to prevent attacks.
options: Add an Amazon Inspector agent to the ALB.
Configure Amazon Macie to prevent attacks.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced to prevent attacks.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to monitor the ALB.
cards.explanation: Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS protection for ALB with 24/7 DRT support, advanced mitigations, and cost protection. Inspector (A) is vulnerability scanning. Macie (B) is PII discovery. GuardDuty (D) is threat detection but doesn't actively mitigate DDoS. Mental shortcut: 'reduce DDoS risk on ALB' = Shield Advanced.
tricks: 'reduce DDoS risk on ALB' = Shield Advanced
'DDoS protection' = AWS Shield (Standard free, Advanced paid + 24/7 DRT)

cards.q: A company’s web application is running on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The company recently changed its policy, which now requires the application to be accessed from one specific country only. Which configuration will meet this requirement?
cards.a: C. Configure AWS WAF on the Application Load Balancer in a VPC.
options: Configure the security group for the EC2 instances.
Configure the security group on the Application Load Balancer.
Configure AWS WAF on the Application Load Balancer in a VPC.
Configure the network ACL for the subnet that contains the EC2 instances.
cards.explanation: AWS WAF on the ALB supports geo-match rules to allow traffic only from a specific country and block all others. Security groups (A, B) don't support country-level filtering, only IP/port. NACLs (D) also don't have country awareness. Mental shortcut: 'allow only one country + ALB' = AWS WAF geo-match.
tricks: 'allow only one country + ALB' = AWS WAF geo-match

cards.q: A company provides an API to its users that automates inquiries for tax computations based on item prices. The company experiences a larger number of inquiries during the holiday season only that cause slower response times. A solutions architect needs to design a solution that is scalable and elastic. What should the solutions architect do to accomplish this?
cards.a: B. Design a REST API using Amazon API Gateway that accepts the item names. API Gateway passes item names to AWS Lambda for tax computations.
options: Provide an API hosted on an Amazon EC2 instance. The EC2 instance performs the required computations when the API request is made.
Design a REST API using Amazon API Gateway that accepts the item names. API Gateway passes item names to AWS Lambda for tax computations.
Create an Application Load Balancer that has two Amazon EC2 instances behind it. The EC2 instances will compute the tax on the received item names.
Design a REST API using Amazon API Gateway that connects with an API hosted on an Amazon EC2 instance. API Gateway accepts and passes the item names to the EC2 instance for tax computations.
cards.explanation: API Gateway + Lambda is fully serverless and scales automatically with traffic, perfect for seasonal spikes (holiday) with no idle compute cost. EC2 (A, C, D) requires capacity planning and idle compute outside the holiday season. Mental shortcut: 'seasonal API + scale and elastic' = API Gateway + Lambda.
tricks: 'seasonal API + scale and elastic' = API Gateway + Lambda

cards.q: A solutions architect is creating a new Amazon CloudFront distribution for an application. Some of the information submitted by users is sensitive. The application uses HTTPS but needs another layer of security. The sensitive information should.be protected throughout the entire application stack, and access to the information should be restricted to certain applications. Which action should the solutions architect take?
cards.a: C. Configure a CloudFront field-level encryption profile.
options: Configure a CloudFront signed URL.
Configure a CloudFront signed cookie.
Configure a CloudFront field-level encryption profile.
Configure CloudFront and set the Origin Protocol Policy setting to HTTPS Only for the Viewer Protocol Policy.
cards.explanation: CloudFront field-level encryption encrypts specific sensitive fields with a public key at the edge so only authorized backend services with the corresponding private key can decrypt. End-to-end protection beyond TLS. Signed URLs/cookies (A, B) restrict access to content, not encrypt fields. Origin Protocol HTTPS Only (D) protects in-transit between CloudFront and origin, not the field content end to end. Mental shortcut: 'protect sensitive form fields end-to-end through entire stack' = CloudFront field-level encryption.
tricks: 'protect sensitive form fields end-to-end through entire stack' = CloudFront field-level encryption
'reduce latency for global users' = CloudFront edge caching

cards.q: A gaming company hosts a browser-based application on AWS. The users of the application consume a large number of videos and images that are stored in Amazon S3. This content is the same for all users. The application has increased in popularity, and millions of users worldwide accessing these media files. The company wants to provide the files to the users while reducing the load on the origin. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: B. Deploy an Amazon CloudFront web distribution in front of the S3 bucket.
options: Deploy an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator in front of the web servers.
Deploy an Amazon CloudFront web distribution in front of the S3 bucket.
Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis instance in front of the web servers.
Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached instance in front of the web servers.
cards.explanation: CloudFront caches S3 static media at edge globally, drastically reducing origin S3 requests and giving users low-latency access. Cheapest. Global Accelerator (A) is for non-HTTP, no caching. ElastiCache (C, D) is for app-level caching of DB results, not static media files. Mental shortcut: 'reduce origin S3 load + global static media' = CloudFront.
tricks: 'reduce origin S3 load + global static media' = CloudFront

cards.q: A company has a multi-tier application that runs six front-end web servers in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group in a single Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). A solutions architect needs to modify the infrastructure to be highly available without modifying the application. Which architecture should the solutions architect choose that provides high availability?
cards.a: B. Modify the Auto Scaling group to use three instances across each of two Availability Zones.
options: Create an Auto Scaling group that uses three instances across each of two Regions.
Modify the Auto Scaling group to use three instances across each of two Availability Zones.
Create an Auto Scaling template that can be used to quickly create more instances in another Region.
Change the ALB in front of the Amazon EC2 instances in a round-robin configuration to balance traffic to the web tier.
cards.explanation: Single AZ = single point of failure. Multi-AZ within the same Region (3 instances per AZ across 2 AZs) makes the existing app HA without code changes. Multi-Region (A, C) is more change than required and adds cross-Region complexity. Round-robin (D) doesn't add resilience to AZ failures. Mental shortcut: 'add HA without modifying app + EC2 + ASG' = Multi-AZ in the same Region.
tricks: 'add HA without modifying app + EC2 + ASG' = Multi-AZ in the same Region

cards.q: An ecommerce company has an order-processing application that uses Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function. The application stores data in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. During a recent sales event, a sudden surge in customer orders occurred. Some customers experienced timeouts, and the application did not process the orders of those customers. A solutions architect determined that the CPU utilization and memory utilization were high on the database because of a large number of open connections. The solutions architect needs to prevent the timeout errors while making the least possible changes to the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Use Amazon RDS Proxy to create a proxy for the database. Modify the Lambda function to use the RDS Proxy endpoint instead of the database endpoint.
options: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function. Modify the database to be a global database in multiple AWS Regions.
Use Amazon RDS Proxy to create a proxy for the database. Modify the Lambda function to use the RDS Proxy endpoint instead of the database endpoint.
Create a read replica for the database in a different AWS Region. Use query string parameters in API Gateway to route traffic to the read replica.
Migrate the data from Aurora PostgreSQL to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Modify the Lambda function to use the DynamoDB table.
cards.explanation: RDS Proxy maintains a pool of warm DB connections shared across Lambda invocations, eliminating the connection storms that overwhelm Aurora. Minimal app changes (just point Lambda at the proxy endpoint). Provisioned concurrency (A) reduces cold starts but doesn't address connection saturation. Read replica via API Gateway routing (C) is high-effort and reads not the issue. Migrating to DynamoDB (D) is massive app rewrite. Mental shortcut: 'Lambda + Aurora connection storm' = RDS Proxy.
tricks: 'Lambda + Aurora connection storm' = RDS Proxy

cards.q: An application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The application needs to access an Amazon DynamoDB table. What is the MOST secure way to access the table while ensuring that the traffic does not leave the AWS network?
cards.a: A. Use a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB.
options: Use a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB.
Use a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
Use a NAT instance in a private subnet.
Use the internet gateway attached to the VPC.
cards.explanation: VPC gateway endpoint for DynamoDB keeps traffic on the AWS network, no Internet, no NAT, free. NAT (B, C) sends traffic via the public Internet. IGW (D) requires Internet path. Mental shortcut: 'private EC2 to DynamoDB + no Internet' = VPC gateway endpoint.
tricks: 'private EC2 to DynamoDB + no Internet' = VPC gateway endpoint

cards.q: An entertainment company is using Amazon DynamoDB to store media metadata. The application is read intensive and experiencing delays. The company does not have staff to handle additional operational overhead and needs to improve the performance efficiency of DynamoDB without reconfiguring the application. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement?
cards.a: B. Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
options: Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.
Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
Replicate data by using DynamoDB global tables.
Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with Auto Discovery enabled.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed in-memory cache for DynamoDB, sits in front, requires only swapping the SDK call to point at the DAX cluster (minimal app change, but the question says 'without reconfiguring' which DAX still satisfies because the application keeps DynamoDB API). ElastiCache Redis or Memcached (A, D) requires custom cache invalidation logic. Global tables (C) is multi-Region replication, doesn't speed up reads in one Region. Mental shortcut: 'speed up DynamoDB reads + LEAST app change' = DAX.
tricks: 'speed up DynamoDB reads + LEAST app change' = DAX

cards.q: A company’s infrastructure consists of Amazon EC2 instances and an Amazon RDS DB instance in a single AWS Region. The company wants to back up its data in a separate Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
cards.a: A. Use AWS Backup to copy EC2 backups and RDS backups to the separate Region.
options: Use AWS Backup to copy EC2 backups and RDS backups to the separate Region.
Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM) to copy EC2 backups and RDS backups to the separate Region.
Create Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) of the EC2 instances. Copy the AMIs to the separate Region. Create a read replica for the RDS DB instance in the separate Region.

Create Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots. Copy the EBS snapshots to the separate Region. Create RDS snapshots. Export the RDS snapshots to Amazon S3. Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to the separate Region.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup natively handles EC2 (EBS) backups, RDS backups, and cross-Region copy from a single managed service with backup plans and policies. DLM (B) only manages EBS snapshots. Manual AMIs + RDS replicas (C) is multi-step ops. Manual EBS snapshots + RDS export to S3 + S3 CRR (D) is multiple manual pipelines. Mental shortcut: 'cross-Region backup of EC2 + RDS + LEAST ops' = AWS Backup.
tricks: 'cross-Region backup of EC2 + RDS + LEAST ops' = AWS Backup
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A solutions architect needs to securely store a database user name and password that an application uses to access an Amazon RDS DB instance. The application that accesses the database runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. The solutions architect wants to create a secure parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
cards.a: A. Create an IAM role that has read access to the Parameter Store parameter. Allow Decrypt access to an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key that is used to encrypt the parameter. Assign this IAM role to the EC2 instance.
options: Create an IAM role that has read access to the Parameter Store parameter. Allow Decrypt access to an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key that is used to encrypt the parameter. Assign this IAM role to the EC2 instance.

Create an IAM policy that allows read access to the Parameter Store parameter. Allow Decrypt access to an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key that is used to encrypt the parameter. Assign this IAM policy to the EC2 instance.
Create an IAM trust relationship between the Parameter Store parameter and the EC2 instance. Specify Amazon RDS as a principal in the trust policy.
Create an IAM trust relationship between the DB instance and the EC2 instance. Specify Systems Manager as a principal in the trust policy.
cards.explanation: Always create an IAM ROLE for EC2 (not an IAM policy attached directly, EC2 uses roles via instance profile). The role has read access to the parameter and Decrypt access to the KMS key that encrypts the SecureString parameter. IAM policy attached directly to EC2 (B) isn't possible, EC2 needs a role. Trust relationships (C, D) misuse the trust concept (trust policies define who can assume the role, not what it can do). Mental shortcut: 'EC2 access to AWS resource' = IAM role with appropriate permissions assigned via instance profile.
tricks: 'EC2 access to AWS resource' = IAM role with appropriate permissions assigned via instance profile

cards.q: A company is designing a cloud communications platform that is driven by APIs. The application is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB). The company uses Amazon API Gateway to provide external users with access to the application through APIs. The company wants to protect the platform against web exploits like SQL injection and also wants to detect and mitigate large, sophisticated DDoS attacks. Which combination of solutions provides the MOST protection? (Choose two.)
cards.a: B. Use AWS Shield Advanced with the NLB. ; C. Use AWS WAF to protect Amazon API Gateway.
options: Use AWS WAF to protect the NLB.
Use AWS Shield Advanced with the NLB.
Use AWS WAF to protect Amazon API Gateway.
Use Amazon GuardDuty with AWS Shield Standard
Use AWS Shield Standard with Amazon API Gateway.
cards.explanation: WAF on API Gateway (C) protects against SQL injection and XSS at the edge. Shield Advanced on the NLB (B) provides large-scale DDoS protection. WAF cannot attach to NLB (A) since WAF works on HTTP-based services. GuardDuty + Shield Standard (D) is detection + free DDoS layer 3/4 only, doesn't mitigate large attacks. Shield Standard on API Gateway (E) is automatic, doesn't add advanced mitigations. Mental shortcut: 'web exploits + sophisticated DDoS' = WAF on API Gateway + Shield Advanced on NLB.
tricks: 'web exploits + sophisticated DDoS' = WAF on API Gateway + Shield Advanced on NLB
'SQL injection / XSS protection' = AWS WAF managed rule groups
'DDoS protection' = AWS Shield (Standard free, Advanced paid + 24/7 DRT)

cards.q: A company has a legacy data processing application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Data is processed sequentially, but the order of results does not matter. The application uses a monolithic architecture. The only way that the company can scale the application to meet increased demand is to increase the size of the instances.
