Create an accelerator by using AWS Global Accelerator, and register the NLBs as its endpoints. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the accelerator DNS.
options: Configure three Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. Create an accelerator by using AWS Global Accelerator, and register the NLBs as its endpoints. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the accelerator DNS.

Configure three Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. Create an accelerator by using AWS Global Accelerator, and register the ALBs as its endpoints. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the accelerator DNS.

Configure three Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. In Route 53, create a latency-based record that points to the three NLBs, and use it as an origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the CloudFront DNS.

Configure three Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in the three AWS Regions to address the on-premises endpoints. In Route 53, create a latency-based record that points to the three ALBs, and use it as an origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Provide access to the application by using a CNAME that points to the CloudFront DNS.
cards.explanation: Global Accelerator with NLBs that point to the on-premises endpoints provides anycast IPs over the AWS backbone for low-latency UDP-friendly routing. NLB supports UDP (B's ALB doesn't). CloudFront (C, D) doesn't support UDP. Mental shortcut: 'on-prem app behind AWS edge + UDP + multi-Region acceleration' = Global Accelerator + NLB.
tricks: 'on-prem app behind AWS edge + UDP + multi-Region acceleration' = Global Accelerator + NLB
'UDP traffic' = NLB only (ALB does NOT support UDP); for global VoIP add Global Accelerator

cards.q: A solutions architect wants all new users to have specific complexity requirements and mandatory rotation periods for IAM user passwords. What should the solutions architect do to accomplish this?
cards.a: A. Set an overall password policy for the entire AWS account.
options: Set an overall password policy for the entire AWS account.
Set a password policy for each IAM user in the AWS account.
Use third-party vendor software to set password requirements.
Attach an Amazon CloudWatch rule to the Create_newuser event to set the password with the appropriate requirements.
cards.explanation: IAM has a single account-wide password policy that applies to all IAM users, configurable for length, complexity, and rotation. Per-user policies (B) don't exist for password complexity. Third-party software (C) is unnecessary. CloudWatch + custom code (D) reinvents the wheel. Mental shortcut: 'IAM password complexity + rotation across all users' = account password policy.
tricks: 'IAM password complexity + rotation across all users' = account password policy

cards.q: A company has migrated an application to Amazon EC2 Linux instances. One of these EC2 instances runs several 1-hour tasks on a schedule. These tasks were written by different teams and have no common programming language. The company is concerned about performance and scalability while these tasks run on a single instance. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to resolve these concerns. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
cards.a: A. Use AWS Batch to run the tasks as jobs. Schedule the jobs by using Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).
options: Use AWS Batch to run the tasks as jobs. Schedule the jobs by using Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).
Convert the EC2 instance to a container. Use AWS App Runner to create the container on demand to run the tasks as jobs.
Copy the tasks into AWS Lambda functions. Schedule the Lambda functions by using Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).
Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the EC2 instance that runs the tasks. Create an Auto Scaling group with the AMI to run multiple copies of the instance.
cards.explanation: AWS Batch runs heterogeneous container/job-defined batch jobs at scale on managed EC2/Fargate, scheduled by EventBridge. Each task can use its own runtime (Java, Python, Node, etc.) via Docker, and Batch handles compute provisioning, queueing, and scaling. App Runner (B) is for HTTP web apps, not batch. Lambda (C) caps at 15 minutes (matches), but rewriting tasks across languages is operational overhead. EC2 ASG (D) is heavy ops. Mental shortcut: 'scheduled batch with mixed runtimes + LEAST overhead' = AWS Batch + EventBridge.
tricks: 'scheduled batch with mixed runtimes + LEAST overhead' = AWS Batch + EventBridge
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A company runs a public three-tier web application in a VPC. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances that run in private subnets need to communicate with a license server over the internet. The company needs a managed solution that minimizes operational maintenance. Which solution meets these requirements?
cards.a: C. Provision a NAT gateway in a public subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT gateway.
options: Provision a NAT instance in a public subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT instance.
Provision a NAT instance in a private subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT instance.
Provision a NAT gateway in a public subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT gateway.
Provision a NAT gateway in a private subnet. Modify each private subnet's route table with a default route that points to the NAT gateway.
cards.explanation: NAT Gateway is the AWS-managed NAT service: deploy in a public subnet, point private subnet route tables to it. Highly available within an AZ, no patching, no servers. NAT instance (A, B) is unmanaged EC2 (deprecated pattern). NAT gateway in private subnet (D) doesn't work, it must be in a public subnet. Mental shortcut: 'managed outbound internet access from private subnet' = NAT Gateway in public subnet.
tricks: 'managed outbound internet access from private subnet' = NAT Gateway in public subnet

cards.q: A company needs to create an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster to host a digital media streaming application. The EKS cluster will use a managed node group that is backed by Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes for storage. The company must encrypt all data at rest by using a customer managed key that is stored in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Which combination of actions will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
cards.a: C. Enable EBS encryption by default in the AWS Region where the EKS cluster will be created. Select the customer managed key as the default key. ; D. Create the EKS cluster. Create an IAM role that has a policy that grants permission to the customer managed key. Associate the role with the EKS cluster.
options: Use a Kubernetes plugin that uses the customer managed key to perform data encryption.
After creation of the EKS cluster, locate the EBS volumes. Enable encryption by using the customer managed key.
Enable EBS encryption by default in the AWS Region where the EKS cluster will be created. Select the customer managed key as the default key.
Create the EKS cluster. Create an IAM role that has a policy that grants permission to the customer managed key. Associate the role with the EKS cluster.
Store the customer managed key as a Kubernetes secret in the EKS cluster. Use the customer managed key to encrypt the EBS volumes.
cards.explanation: Enable EBS encryption by default in the Region with the customer-managed KMS key as the default (C): every new EBS volume in the Region is encrypted automatically. Then create the EKS cluster with an IAM role that has permission to use the customer-managed key (D). Kubernetes secret-based encryption (E) and post-creation manual encryption (B) are operational overhead. Plugin (A) is custom. Mental shortcut: 'EKS managed node group EBS encryption with CMK + LEAST overhead' = EBS encryption-by-default + IAM role with KMS access.
tricks: 'EKS managed node group EBS encryption with CMK + LEAST overhead' = EBS encryption-by-default + IAM role with KMS access
'customer managed key' or 'control rotation' = KMS customer managed key (CMK)
'encrypt at rest' = SSE-KMS for full control, SSE-S3 for default, SSE-C if customer holds the key
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A company wants to migrate an Oracle database to AWS. The database consists of a single table that contains millions of geographic information systems (GIS) images that are high resolution and are identified by a geographic code. When a natural disaster occurs, tens of thousands of images get updated every few minutes. Each geographic code has a single image or row that is associated with it. The company wants a solution that is highly available and scalable during such events. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: B. Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Use Amazon DynamoDB with the geographic code as the key and the image S3 URL as the value.
options: Store the images and geographic codes in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.
Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Use Amazon DynamoDB with the geographic code as the key and the image S3 URL as the value.
Store the images and geographic codes in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) during times of high load.
Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Store geographic codes and image S3 URLs in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB single-digit-ms reads/writes scale automatically and handle the burst of tens of thousands of updates/min. Storing the actual high-resolution images in S3 (cheap durable object storage) and using DynamoDB to map geographic code -> S3 URL is the cost-effective pattern. Storing images IN DynamoDB (C) is expensive (DynamoDB charges by item size). Oracle on RDS (A, D) doesn't scale on writes during disaster spikes. Mental shortcut: 'images + key-value index + scale on burst writes + cost' = S3 for images + DynamoDB for index.
tricks: 'images + key-value index + scale on burst writes + cost' = S3 for images + DynamoDB for index

cards.q: A company has an application that collects data from IoT sensors on automobiles. The data is streamed and stored in Amazon S3 through Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose. The data produces trillions of S3 objects each year. Each morning, the company uses the data from the previous 30 days to retrain a suite of machine learning (ML) models. Four times each year, the company uses the data from the previous 12 months to perform analysis and train other ML models. The data must be available with minimal delay for up to 1 year. After 1 year, the data must be retained for archival purposes. Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: D. Use the S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days, and then to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.
options: Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.
Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically move objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.
Use the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.

Use the S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days, and then to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year.
cards.explanation: 30-day window of frequent access fits S3 Standard. After 30 days, transition to Standard-IA (still ms access for the 4x/year analysis but cheaper). After 1 year, transition to Deep Archive for cheap long-term retention. Intelligent-Tiering (A, B) charges per-object monitoring fees that aren't worth it when access patterns are clearly defined. Standard-IA from day 1 (C) overpays for the daily-accessed first 30 days. Mental shortcut: 'known access pattern with 3 phases (hot 30d, cool 11mo, cold archive) + cost-effective' = explicit Lifecycle Standard -> Standard-IA -> Deep Archive.
tricks: 'known access pattern with 3 phases (hot 30d, cool 11mo, cold archive) + cost-effective' = explicit Lifecycle Standard -> Standard-IA -> Deep Archive

cards.q: A company is running several business applications in three separate VPCs within the us-east-1 Region. The applications must be able to communicate between VPCs. The applications also must be able to consistently send hundreds of gigabytes of data each day to a latency- sensitive application that runs in a single on-premises data center. A solutions architect needs to design a network connectivity solution that maximizes cost-effectiveness. Which solution meets these requirements?
cards.a: D. Set up one AWS Direct Connect connection from the data center to AWS. Create a transit gateway, and attach each VPC to the transit gateway. Establish connectivity between the Direct Connect connection and the transit gateway.
options: Configure three AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections from the data center to AWS. Establish connectivity by configuring one VPN connection for each VPC.
Launch a third-party virtual network appliance in each VPC. Establish an IPsec VPN tunnel between the data center and each virtual appliance.
Set up three AWS Direct Connect connections from the data center to a Direct Connect gateway in us-east-1. Establish connectivity by configuring each VPC to use one of the Direct Connect connections.

Set up one AWS Direct Connect connection from the data center to AWS. Create a transit gateway, and attach each VPC to the transit gateway. Establish connectivity between the Direct Connect connection and the transit gateway.
cards.explanation: One Direct Connect connection (consistent low latency for hundreds of GB/day) + Transit Gateway attached to all 3 VPCs gives full inter-VPC routing AND on-prem reachability via the Direct Connect attachment. Three Direct Connects (C) is overkill and costly. VPN (A, B) doesn't deliver consistent low latency for hundreds of GB/day. Mental shortcut: 'multi-VPC + on-prem + low latency + cost-effective' = one Direct Connect + Transit Gateway.
tricks: 'multi-VPC + on-prem + low latency + cost-effective' = one Direct Connect + Transit Gateway

cards.q: An ecommerce company is building a distributed application that involves several serverless functions and AWS services to complete order- processing tasks. These tasks require manual approvals as part of the workflow. A solutions architect needs to design an architecture for the order-processing application. The solution must be able to combine multiple AWS Lambda functions into responsive serverless applications. The solution also must orchestrate data and services that run on Amazon EC2 instances, containers, or on-premises servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
cards.a: A. Use AWS Step Functions to build the application.
options: Use AWS Step Functions to build the application.
Integrate all the application components in an AWS Glue job.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to build the application.
Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EventBridge events to build the application.
cards.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates Lambda + EC2 + container + on-prem services with native support for human approval steps (callback patterns), error handling, and visual workflow. Glue (B) is for ETL workflows. SQS (C) is queueing, not orchestration of multi-step approvals. Lambda + EventBridge (D) can route events but doesn't natively handle multi-step orchestration with manual approvals. Mental shortcut: 'orchestrate Lambda + non-Lambda + manual approvals + LEAST overhead' = Step Functions.
tricks: 'orchestrate Lambda + non-Lambda + manual approvals + LEAST overhead' = Step Functions
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A company has launched an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Most of the connections to the database come from serverless applications. Application traffic to the database changes significantly at random intervals. At times of high demand, users report that their applications experience database connection rejection errors. Which solution will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?
cards.a: A. Create a proxy in RDS Proxy. Configure the users’ applications to use the DB instance through RDS Proxy.
options: Create a proxy in RDS Proxy. Configure the users’ applications to use the DB instance through RDS Proxy.
Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached between the users’ applications and the DB instance.
Migrate the DB instance to a different instance class that has higher I/O capacity. Configure the users’ applications to use the new DB instance.
Configure Multi-AZ for the DB instance. Configure the users’ applications to switch between the DB instances.
cards.explanation: RDS Proxy pools and reuses DB connections, absorbing serverless connection storms during traffic spikes, with zero app code changes (just point to the proxy endpoint). ElastiCache (B) caches read results, doesn't fix DB connection rejection. Larger instance (C) treats the symptom, not the cause. Multi-AZ (D) is HA, doesn't double connection capacity. Mental shortcut: 'serverless connection storms on RDS + LEAST overhead' = RDS Proxy.
tricks: 'serverless connection storms on RDS + LEAST overhead' = RDS Proxy
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A company recently deployed a new auditing system to centralize information about operating system versions, patching, and installed software for Amazon EC2 instances. A solutions architect must ensure all instances provisioned through EC2 Auto Scaling groups successfully send reports to the auditing system as soon as they are launched and terminated. Which solution achieves these goals MOST efficiently?
cards.a: B. Use EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to run a custom script to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.
options: Use a scheduled AWS Lambda function and run a script remotely on all EC2 instances to send data to the audit system.
Use EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to run a custom script to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.
Use an EC2 Auto Scaling launch configuration to run a custom script through user data to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.
Run a custom script on the instance operating system to send data to the audit system. Configure the script to be invoked by the EC2 Auto Scaling group when the instance starts and is terminated.
cards.explanation: Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks pause instances during launch and termination so a custom script can run reliably (e.g., via SSM Run Command or user data) before the instance becomes 'In Service' or fully terminates. The hook waits for completion or timeout. Lambda + remote scripts (A) is brittle and doesn't capture termination cleanly. User data (C) only runs on launch, not on termination. Custom scripts triggered by ASG events (D) is essentially what lifecycle hooks formalize. Mental shortcut: 'run code on instance launch AND termination reliably' = ASG lifecycle hooks.
tricks: 'run code on instance launch AND termination reliably' = ASG lifecycle hooks

cards.q: A company is developing a real-time multiplayer game that uses UDP for communications between the client and servers in an Auto Scaling group. Spikes in demand are anticipated during the day, so the game server platform must adapt accordingly. Developers want to store gamer scores and other non-relational data in a database solution that will scale without intervention. Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?
cards.a: B. Use a Network Load Balancer for traffic distribution and Amazon DynamoDB on-demand for data storage.
options: Use Amazon Route 53 for traffic distribution and Amazon Aurora Serverless for data storage.
Use a Network Load Balancer for traffic distribution and Amazon DynamoDB on-demand for data storage.
Use a Network Load Balancer for traffic distribution and Amazon Aurora Global Database for data storage.
Use an Application Load Balancer for traffic distribution and Amazon DynamoDB global tables for data storage.
cards.explanation: Real-time UDP gaming requires NLB (UDP-capable, ALB is HTTP-only). DynamoDB on-demand scales without intervention to handle gamer score writes. Aurora Serverless (A) is relational, not non-relational. Aurora Global (C) is overkill (single-Region game). DynamoDB global tables (D) is for multi-Region active-active, not requested. Mental shortcut: 'UDP game + non-relational + auto-scale data' = NLB + DynamoDB on-demand.
tricks: 'UDP game + non-relational + auto-scale data' = NLB + DynamoDB on-demand
'UDP traffic' = NLB only (ALB does NOT support UDP); for global VoIP add Global Accelerator

cards.q: A company hosts a frontend application that uses an Amazon API Gateway API backend that is integrated with AWS Lambda. When the API receives requests, the Lambda function loads many libraries. Then the Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database, processes the data, and returns the data to the frontend application. The company wants to ensure that response latency is as low as possible for all its users with the fewest number of changes to the company's operations. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function that handles the requests.
options: Establish a connection between the frontend application and the database to make queries faster by bypassing the API.
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function that handles the requests.
Cache the results of the queries in Amazon S3 for faster retrieval of similar datasets.
Increase the size of the database to increase the number of connections Lambda can establish at one time.
cards.explanation: Lambda provisioned concurrency keeps a defined number of execution environments warm, with libraries pre-loaded, so the first request after an idle period doesn't pay the cold-start penalty (which loading many libraries makes worse). Direct DB connection (A) bypasses business logic, breaks the architecture. S3 cache (C) is a heavy redesign. Bigger DB (D) doesn't fix Lambda cold starts. Mental shortcut: 'reduce Lambda cold start latency + LEAST changes' = provisioned concurrency.
tricks: 'reduce Lambda cold start latency + LEAST changes' = provisioned concurrency

cards.q: A company is migrating its on-premises workload to the AWS Cloud. The company already uses several Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon RDS DB instances. The company wants a solution that automatically starts and stops the EC2 instances and DB instances outside of business hours. The solution must minimize cost and infrastructure maintenance. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: D. Create an AWS Lambda function that will start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function on a schedule.
options: Scale the EC2 instances by using elastic resize. Scale the DB instances to zero outside of business hours.
Explore AWS Marketplace for partner solutions that will automatically start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances on a schedule.
Launch another EC2 instance. Configure a crontab schedule to run shell scripts that will start and stop the existing EC2 instances and DB instances on a schedule.
Create an AWS Lambda function that will start and stop the EC2 instances and DB instances. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function on a schedule.
cards.explanation: Lambda + EventBridge scheduled rules is the canonical serverless way to start/stop EC2 and RDS on a cron-like schedule, fully managed, costs pennies. Marketplace solutions (B) cost money. Cron on a dedicated EC2 (C) needs maintenance. Elastic resize (A) is wrong terminology and doesn't 'scale to zero' on RDS. Mental shortcut: 'scheduled start/stop of EC2 + RDS + LEAST cost and maintenance' = Lambda + EventBridge.
tricks: 'scheduled start/stop of EC2 + RDS + LEAST cost and maintenance' = Lambda + EventBridge

cards.q: A company hosts a three-tier web application that includes a PostgreSQL database. The database stores the metadata from documents. The company searches the metadata for key terms to retrieve documents that the company reviews in a report each month. The documents are stored in Amazon S3. The documents are usually written only once, but they are updated frequently. The reporting process takes a few hours with the use of relational queries. The reporting process must not prevent any document modifications or the addition of new documents. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to speed up the reporting process. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of change to the application code?
cards.a: B. Set up a new Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that includes an Aurora Replica. Issue queries to the Aurora Replica to generate the reports.
options: Set up a new Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) cluster that includes a read replica. Scale the read replica to generate the reports.
Set up a new Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that includes an Aurora Replica. Issue queries to the Aurora Replica to generate the reports.
Set up a new Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the reporting module to query the secondary RDS node so that the reporting module does not affect the primary node.
Set up a new Amazon DynamoDB table to store the documents. Use a fixed write capacity to support new document entries. Automatically scale the read capacity to support the reports.
cards.explanation: Aurora PostgreSQL is fully PostgreSQL-compatible (drop-in for the existing app). Aurora Replicas have very low replication lag and can serve heavy reporting reads without affecting the primary's writes. DocumentDB (A) is not PostgreSQL-compatible, requires app changes. Multi-AZ secondary in RDS (C) cannot be used for read traffic; it's only for failover. DynamoDB (D) is NoSQL, big rewrite. Mental shortcut: 'PostgreSQL + offload heavy reads + minimal change' = Aurora PostgreSQL + Aurora Replica.
tricks: 'PostgreSQL + offload heavy reads + minimal change' = Aurora PostgreSQL + Aurora Replica

cards.q: A company has a three-tier application on AWS that ingests sensor data from its users’ devices. The traffic flows through a Network Load Balancer (NLB), then to Amazon EC2 instances for the web tier, and finally to EC2 instances for the application tier. The application tier makes calls to a database. What should a solutions architect do to improve the security of the data in transit?
cards.a: A. Configure a TLS listener. Deploy the server certificate on the NLB.
options: Configure a TLS listener. Deploy the server certificate on the NLB.
Configure AWS Shield Advanced. Enable AWS WAF on the NLB.
Change the load balancer to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Enable AWS WAF on the ALB.
Encrypt the Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume on the EC2 instances by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).
cards.explanation: NLB supports TLS listeners with server certificates from ACM, terminating TLS at the load balancer for in-transit encryption. Shield/WAF (B, C) protect against attacks but don't encrypt traffic. EBS encryption (D) is at-rest, not in-transit. Mental shortcut: 'encrypt in transit at NLB' = TLS listener with ACM certificate.
tricks: 'encrypt in transit at NLB' = TLS listener with ACM certificate

cards.q: A company is planning to migrate a commercial off-the-shelf application from its on-premises data center to AWS. The software has a software licensing model using sockets and cores with predictable capacity and uptime requirements. The company wants to use its existing licenses, which were purchased earlier this year. Which Amazon EC2 pricing option is the MOST cost-effective?
cards.a: A. Dedicated Reserved Hosts
options: Dedicated Reserved Hosts
Dedicated On-Demand Hosts
Dedicated Reserved Instances
Dedicated On-Demand Instances
cards.explanation: Dedicated Hosts give you visibility and control over the physical socket/core layout, required for socket/core-based BYOL licensing. Reserved (1- or 3-year commitment) is most cost-effective for predictable always-on workloads. Dedicated Instances (C, D) provide hardware isolation but not socket/core visibility for BYOL. Mental shortcut: 'BYOL on sockets/cores + predictable + cost-effective' = Dedicated Reserved Hosts.
tricks: 'BYOL on sockets/cores + predictable + cost-effective' = Dedicated Reserved Hosts

cards.q: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 Linux instances across multiple Availability Zones. The application needs a storage layer that is highly available and Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX)-compliant. The storage layer must provide maximum data durability and must be shareable across the EC2 instances. The data in the storage layer will be accessed frequently for the first 30 days and will be accessed infrequently after that time. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: C. Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (EFS Standard-IA).
options: Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Glacier.
Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move infrequently accessed data to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).
Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (EFS Standard-IA).
Use the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) One Zone storage class. Create a lifecycle management policy to move infrequently accessed data to EFS One Zone-Infrequent Access (EFS One Zone-IA).
cards.explanation: EFS provides shared POSIX file storage across multiple EC2 instances, multi-AZ, with EFS Lifecycle Management auto-tiering rarely accessed files to EFS Standard-IA at significantly lower cost. S3 (A, B) is not POSIX. EFS One Zone (D) sacrifices multi-AZ resilience. Mental shortcut: 'shared POSIX across EC2 + lifecycle for cold data + max durability' = EFS Standard + lifecycle to EFS Standard-IA.
tricks: 'shared POSIX across EC2 + lifecycle for cold data + max durability' = EFS Standard + lifecycle to EFS Standard-IA

cards.q: A solutions architect is creating a new VPC design. There are two public subnets for the load balancer, two private subnets for web servers, and two private subnets for MySQL. The web servers use only HTTPS. The solutions architect has already created a security group for the load balancer allowing port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Company policy requires that each resource has the least access required to still be able to perform its tasks. Which additional configuration strategy should the solutions architect use to meet these requirements?
cards.a: C. Create a security group for the web servers and allow port 443 from the load balancer. Create a security group for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
options: Create a security group for the web servers and allow port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Create a security group for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
Create a network ACL for the web servers and allow port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Create a network ACL for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
Create a security group for the web servers and allow port 443 from the load balancer. Create a security group for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
Create a network ACL for the web servers and allow port 443 from the load balancer. Create a network ACL for the MySQL servers and allow port 3306 from the web servers security group.
cards.explanation: Least privilege at the network layer: web SG allows 443 only from the load balancer SG (not from 0.0.0.0/0), and the MySQL SG allows 3306 only from the web SG. Allowing 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on web servers (A) violates least privilege because traffic should only come from the LB. NACLs (B, D) are stateless and harder to manage at this layer than SGs. Mental shortcut: 'tier-to-tier least privilege' = SG referencing the upstream SG, not CIDR ranges.
tricks: 'tier-to-tier least privilege' = SG referencing the upstream SG, not CIDR ranges

cards.q: An ecommerce company is running a multi-tier application on AWS. The front-end and backend tiers both run on Amazon EC2, and the database runs on Amazon RDS for MySQL. The backend tier communicates with the RDS instance. There are frequent calls to return identical datasets from the database that are causing performance slowdowns. Which action should be taken to improve the performance of the backend?
cards.a: B. Implement Amazon ElastiCache to cache the large datasets.
options: Implement Amazon SNS to store the database calls.
Implement Amazon ElastiCache to cache the large datasets.
Implement an RDS for MySQL read replica to cache database calls.
Implement Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the calls to the database.
cards.explanation: ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) caches the 'identical datasets' returned from MySQL, so repeated reads hit the cache instead of the DB. Read replica (C) helps but the question says 'identical datasets' which is a perfect cache hit pattern, not a replica problem. SNS (A) is pub/sub, not caching. Firehose (D) is for streaming data ingestion. Mental shortcut: 'frequently repeated DB reads + improve performance' = ElastiCache.
tricks: 'frequently repeated DB reads + improve performance' = ElastiCache

cards.q: A new employee has joined a company as a deployment engineer. The deployment engineer will be using AWS CloudFormation templates to create multiple AWS resources. A solutions architect wants the deployment engineer to perform job activities while following the principle of least privilege. Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to accomplish this goal? (Choose two.)
cards.a: D. Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has an IAM policy that allows AWS CloudFormation actions only. ; E. Create an IAM role for the deployment engineer to explicitly define the permissions specific to the AWS CloudFormation stack and launch stacks using that IAM role.
options: Have the deployment engineer use AWS account root user credentials for performing AWS CloudFormation stack operations.
Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has the PowerUsers IAM policy attached.
Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has the AdministratorAccess IAM policy attached.
Create a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and add the IAM user to a group that has an IAM policy that allows AWS CloudFormation actions only.
Create an IAM role for the deployment engineer to explicitly define the permissions specific to the AWS CloudFormation stack and launch stacks using that IAM role.
cards.explanation: Least privilege for a CloudFormation deployment engineer: create an IAM user (D) in a group with a policy that ONLY allows CloudFormation actions (and the actions needed inside the stacks via a service role). Then create an IAM role (E) used by the CloudFormation stack itself with the specific permissions to provision resources, so the user doesn't get those permissions directly. Root credentials (A) are forbidden. PowerUser (B) and AdministratorAccess (C) are too broad. Mental shortcut: 'CloudFormation user + least privilege' = scoped IAM user + IAM role for the CloudFormation service.
tricks: 'CloudFormation user + least privilege' = scoped IAM user + IAM role for the CloudFormation service
'least privilege' = scope IAM permissions to specific resources/actions, not *

cards.q: A company is deploying a two-tier web application in a VPC. The web tier is using an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with public subnets that span multiple Availability Zones. The database tier consists of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in separate private subnets. The web tier requires access to the database to retrieve product information. The web application is not working as intended. The web application reports that it cannot connect to the database. The database is confirmed to be up and running. All configurations for the network ACLs, security groups, and route tables are still in their default states. What should a solutions architect recommend to fix the application?
cards.a: D. Add an inbound rule to the security group of the database tier’s RDS instance to allow traffic from the web tiers security group.
options: Add an explicit rule to the private subnet’s network ACL to allow traffic from the web tier’s EC2 instances.
Add a route in the VPC route table to allow traffic between the web tier’s EC2 instances and the database tier.
Deploy the web tier's EC2 instances and the database tier’s RDS instance into two separate VPCs, and configure VPC peering.
Add an inbound rule to the security group of the database tier’s RDS instance to allow traffic from the web tiers security group.
cards.explanation: By default, security groups deny all inbound traffic. The DB tier SG needs an inbound rule allowing 3306 from the web tier's SG. NACLs (A) are stateless and the default already allows all (it's not the issue). Route table (B) is fine since both are in the same VPC. Separate VPCs + peering (C) is overkill. Mental shortcut: 'EC2 cannot reach RDS in same VPC' = inbound SG rule on the DB SG referencing the web SG.
tricks: 'EC2 cannot reach RDS in same VPC' = inbound SG rule on the DB SG referencing the web SG

cards.q: A company has a large dataset for its online advertising business stored in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in a single Availability Zone. The company wants business reporting queries to run without impacting the write operations to the production DB instance. Which solution meets these requirements?
cards.a: A. Deploy RDS read replicas to process the business reporting queries.
options: Deploy RDS read replicas to process the business reporting queries.
Scale out the DB instance horizontally by placing it behind an Elastic Load Balancer.
Scale up the DB instance to a larger instance type to handle write operations and queries.
Deploy the DB instance in multiple Availability Zones to process the business reporting queries.
cards.explanation: Read replicas offload read-heavy reporting queries from the primary, with replication and minimal lag, so writes on the production DB are not impacted. Horizontal scale via ELB (B) is not how RDS works. Bigger instance (C) doesn't separate read from write workloads. Multi-AZ (D) standby cannot serve reads. Mental shortcut: 'reporting reads without impacting writes' = RDS read replica.
tricks: 'reporting reads without impacting writes' = RDS read replica

cards.q: A company hosts a three-tier ecommerce application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). All ecommerce data is stored in an Amazon RDS for MariaDB Multi-AZ DB instance. The company wants to optimize customer session management during transactions. The application must store session data durably. Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
cards.a: B. Use an Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer session information. ; D. Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to store customer session information.
options: Turn on the sticky sessions feature (session affinity) on the ALB.
Use an Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer session information.
Deploy an Amazon Cognito user pool to manage user session information.
Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to store customer session information.
Use AWS Systems Manager Application Manager in the application to manage user session information.
cards.explanation: Two valid solutions for durable session storage: DynamoDB table (B) for low-latency persistent session items, or ElastiCache for Redis (D) for sub-ms session reads with persistence enabled. Sticky sessions on the ALB (A) just keeps a user on one EC2 instance, doesn't store data durably (instance failure = session loss). Cognito (C) is for user identity, not session payload storage. SSM Application Manager (E) doesn't store session data. Mental shortcut: 'durable session storage' = DynamoDB or ElastiCache for Redis.
tricks: 'durable session storage' = DynamoDB or ElastiCache for Redis

cards.q: A company needs a backup strategy for its three-tier stateless web application. The web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a dynamic scaling policy that is configured to respond to scaling events. The database tier runs on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The web application does not require temporary local storage on the EC2 instances. The company’s recovery point objective (RPO) is 2 hours. The backup strategy must maximize scalability and optimize resource utilization for this environment. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: C. Retain the latest Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) of the web and application tiers. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO.
options: Take snapshots of Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes of the EC2 instances and database every 2 hours to meet the RPO.
Configure a snapshot lifecycle policy to take Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS to meet the RPO.
Retain the latest Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) of the web and application tiers. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO.
Take snapshots of Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes of the EC2 instances every 2 hours. Enable automated backups in Amazon RDS and use point-in-time recovery to meet the RPO.
cards.explanation: Stateless EC2 web tier with no local data means you don't need EBS snapshots; just keep the latest AMI to relaunch. RDS automated backups + PITR cover the 2-hour RPO without managing snapshot schedules manually. Snapshots every 2h (A, B, D) are wasted because the EC2s have no important local state. Mental shortcut: 'stateless EC2 + RDS + 2h RPO + scalable' = AMI for the web tier + RDS automated backups + PITR.
tricks: 'stateless EC2 + RDS + 2h RPO + scalable' = AMI for the web tier + RDS automated backups + PITR
'unpredictable bursty traffic' = Dynamic (Target Tracking) Scaling on CPU/requests

cards.q: A company wants to deploy a new public web application on AWS. The application includes a web server tier that uses Amazon EC2 instances. The application also includes a database tier that uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. The application must be secure and accessible for global customers that have dynamic IP addresses. How should a solutions architect configure the security groups to meet these requirements?
cards.a: A. Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.
options: Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the security group of the web servers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from the IP addresses of the customers. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from the IP addresses of the customers.

Configure the security group for the web servers to allow inbound traffic on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Configure the security group for the DB instance to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0.
cards.explanation: Global customers with dynamic IPs need 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443 for the public web tier. The DB security group should reference the web tier's SG (not customer IPs) so only the web servers can talk to the DB. Restricting customer IPs on the web SG (B, C) doesn't work for dynamic IPs. Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 to the DB (D) exposes MySQL to the internet, never. Mental shortcut: 'public web + private DB' = 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on web SG, 3306 from web SG on DB SG.
tricks: 'public web + private DB' = 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on web SG, 3306 from web SG on DB SG

cards.q: A payment processing company records all voice communication with its customers and stores the audio files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs to capture the text from the audio files. The company must remove from the text any personally identifiable information (PII) that belongs to customers. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
cards.a: C. Configure an Amazon Transcribe transcription job with PII redaction turned on. When an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, invoke an AWS Lambda function to start the transcription job. Store the output in a separate S3 bucket.
options: Process the audio files by using Amazon Kinesis Video Streams. Use an AWS Lambda function to scan for known PII patterns.
When an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, invoke an AWS Lambda function to start an Amazon Textract task to analyze the call recordings.

Configure an Amazon Transcribe transcription job with PII redaction turned on. When an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, invoke an AWS Lambda function to start the transcription job. Store the output in a separate S3 bucket.

Create an Amazon Connect contact flow that ingests the audio files with transcription turned on. Embed an AWS Lambda function to scan for known PII patterns. Use Amazon EventBridge to start the contact flow when an audio file is uploaded to the S3 bucket.
cards.explanation: Amazon Transcribe natively supports automatic PII redaction in the transcription output. S3 PUT triggers Lambda to start a Transcribe job with PII redaction enabled and the redacted text lands in another S3 bucket. Kinesis Video Streams (A) is for live video, not stored audio. Textract (B) is for documents/images, not audio. Connect contact flow (D) is for live calls in Connect, not batch processing of stored recordings. Mental shortcut: 'audio to text + remove PII' = Amazon Transcribe with PII redaction.
tricks: 'audio to text + remove PII' = Amazon Transcribe with PII redaction
'discover PII in S3' = Amazon Macie (NOT GuardDuty, NOT Inspector)

cards.q: A company is running a multi-tier ecommerce web application in the AWS Cloud. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances with an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Amazon RDS is configured with the latest generation DB instance with 2,000 GB of storage in a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. The database performance affects the application during periods of high demand. A database administrator analyzes the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs and discovers that the application performance always degrades when the number of read and write IOPS is higher than 20,000. What should a solutions architect do to improve the application performance?
cards.a: C. Replace the volume with a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume.
options: Replace the volume with a magnetic volume.
Increase the number of IOPS on the gp3 volume.
Replace the volume with a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume.
Replace the 2,000 GB gp3 volume with two 1,000 GB gp3 volumes.
cards.explanation: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2/io2 Block Express) supports sustained high IOPS (up to 256,000 per volume on io2 Block Express) and consistent sub-ms latency, the right choice when gp3 is hitting its ceiling at 20,000 IOPS. Magnetic (A) is way slower. Bumping gp3 IOPS (B) caps at 16,000 IOPS for general gp3 (the question implies gp3 is already maxed). Two volumes (D) doesn't help RDS, RDS uses one volume. Mental shortcut: 'sustained > 16,000 IOPS' = io2 / io2 Block Express.
tricks: 'sustained > 16,000 IOPS' = io2 / io2 Block Express

cards.q: An IAM user made several configuration changes to AWS resources in their company's account during a production deployment last week. A solutions architect learned that a couple of security group rules are not configured as desired. The solutions architect wants to confirm which IAM user was responsible for making changes. Which service should the solutions architect use to find the desired information?
cards.a: C. AWS CloudTrail
options: Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Inspector
AWS CloudTrail
AWS Config
cards.explanation: CloudTrail records every AWS API call (who, when, what), including security group rule changes, with the IAM identity that made the call. GuardDuty (A) is threat detection, not change attribution. Inspector (B) is vulnerability scanning. Config (D) tracks resource configuration over time but the canonical 'who made this change' answer is CloudTrail event history. Mental shortcut: 'who made this change' = AWS CloudTrail.
tricks: 'who made this change' = AWS CloudTrail

cards.q: A company has implemented a self-managed DNS service on AWS. The solution consists of the following: • Amazon EC2 instances in different AWS Regions • Endpoints of a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator The company wants to protect the solution against DDoS attacks. What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
cards.a: A. Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the accelerator as a resource to protect.
options: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the accelerator as a resource to protect.
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced. Add the EC2 instances as resources to protect.
Create an AWS WAF web ACL that includes a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the accelerator.
Create an AWS WAF web ACL that includes a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the EC2 instances.
cards.explanation: Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS protection for Global Accelerator, ELB, CloudFront, EIP, and Route 53. Adding the accelerator as a protected resource gets you 24/7 DRT (DDoS Response Team), cost protection, and advanced layer 3/4 + layer 7 mitigations. WAF (C, D) is for HTTP-layer attacks; the accelerator's standard service is layer 3/4. Protecting EC2 directly (B) doesn't fit (Shield Advanced doesn't protect bare EC2; you protect the public-facing entry point, the accelerator). Mental shortcut: 'DDoS protection for Global Accelerator' = Shield Advanced on the accelerator.
tricks: 'DDoS protection for Global Accelerator' = Shield Advanced on the accelerator
'DDoS protection' = AWS Shield (Standard free, Advanced paid + 24/7 DRT)

cards.q: An ecommerce company needs to run a scheduled daily job to aggregate and filter sales records for analytics. The company stores the sales records in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each object can be up to 10 GB in size. Based on the number of sales events, the job can take up to an hour to complete. The CPU and memory usage of the job are constant and are known in advance. A solutions architect needs to minimize the amount of operational effort that is needed for the job to run. Which solution meets these requirements?
cards.a: C. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with an AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event that launches an ECS task on the cluster to run the job.
options: Create an AWS Lambda function that has an Amazon EventBridge notification. Schedule the EventBridge event to run once a day.

Create an AWS Lambda function. Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API, and integrate the API with the function. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event that calls the API and invokes the function.
Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with an AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event that launches an ECS task on the cluster to run the job.

Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with an Amazon EC2 launch type and an Auto Scaling group with at least one EC2 instance. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event that launches an ECS task on the cluster to run the job.
cards.explanation: ECS Fargate scheduled task gives you long-running (up to several hours), CPU/memory-known batch jobs without managing servers, scheduled by EventBridge. Lambda (A, B) caps at 15 minutes and may not fit a 1-hour job. ECS on EC2 with ASG (D) is more operational overhead. Mental shortcut: 'scheduled long-running batch + LEAST overhead + known capacity' = ECS Fargate scheduled task.
tricks: 'scheduled long-running batch + LEAST overhead + known capacity' = ECS Fargate scheduled task

cards.q: A company needs to transfer 600 TB of data from its on-premises network-attached storage (NAS) system to the AWS Cloud. The data transfer must be complete within 2 weeks. The data is sensitive and must be encrypted in transit. The company’s internet connection can support an upload speed of 100 Mbps. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
cards.a: C. Use the AWS Snow Family console to order several AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Use the devices to transfer the data to Amazon S3.
options: Use Amazon S3 multi-part upload functionality to transfer the files over HTTPS.
Create a VPN connection between the on-premises NAS system and the nearest AWS Region. Transfer the data over the VPN connection.
Use the AWS Snow Family console to order several AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Use the devices to transfer the data to Amazon S3.
Set up a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection between the company location and the nearest AWS Region. Transfer the data over a VPN connection into the Region to store the data in Amazon S3.
cards.explanation: 600 TB at 100 Mbps takes ~600 days, way beyond 2 weeks. Snowball Edge devices (each 80 TB usable) ship physically, encrypted, and 8 devices in parallel transfer 600 TB in days. Multi-part HTTPS upload (A) and VPN (B) are network-bound. Direct Connect (D) takes weeks to provision and 10 Gbps would still be very expensive vs Snowball for one-time. Mental shortcut: '600 TB + 2 weeks + cost-effective' = parallel Snowball Edge devices.
tricks: '600 TB + 2 weeks + cost-effective' = parallel Snowball Edge devices

cards.q: A financial company hosts a web application on AWS. The application uses an Amazon API Gateway Regional API endpoint to give users the ability to retrieve current stock prices. The company’s security team has noticed an increase in the number of API requests. The security team is concerned that HTTP flood attacks might take the application offline. A solutions architect must design a solution to protect the application from this type of attack. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
cards.a: B. Create a Regional AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the API Gateway stage.
options: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint with a maximum TTL of 24 hours.
Create a Regional AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the API Gateway stage.
Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor the Count metric and alert the security team when the predefined rate is reached.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with Lambda@Edge in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint. Create an AWS Lambda function to block requests from IP addresses that exceed the predefined rate.
cards.explanation: AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule, attached to the API Gateway stage, blocks IPs that exceed a request rate threshold. This is the canonical HTTP-flood/DDoS L7 protection for API Gateway with zero custom code. CloudFront with TTL (A) doesn't block floods. CloudWatch alarms (C) are reactive, manual response. Lambda@Edge custom rate-limiting (D) reinvents what AWS WAF rate-based rules do natively. Mental shortcut: 'HTTP flood protection on API Gateway + LEAST overhead' = AWS WAF rate-based rule.
tricks: 'HTTP flood protection on API Gateway + LEAST overhead' = AWS WAF rate-based rule
'LEAST operational overhead' = pick the most managed/serverless option (Lambda > Fargate > ECS-EC2 > EC2)

cards.q: A meteorological startup company has a custom web application to sell weather data to its users online. The company uses Amazon DynamoDB to store its data and wants to build a new service that sends an alert to the managers of four internal teams every time a new weather event is recorded. The company does not want this new service to affect the performance of the current application. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
cards.a: C. Enable Amazon DynamoDB Streams on the table. Use triggers to write to a single Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to which the teams can subscribe.
options: Use DynamoDB transactions to write new event data to the table. Configure the transactions to notify internal teams.
Have the current application publish a message to four Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topics. Have each team subscribe to one topic.
Enable Amazon DynamoDB Streams on the table. Use triggers to write to a single Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to which the teams can subscribe.

Add a custom attribute to each record to flag new items. Write a cron job that scans the table every minute for items that are new and notifies an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to which the teams can subscribe.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB Streams + Lambda trigger + SNS topic with 4 team subscriptions: every new event triggers a Lambda that publishes once to SNS, fanning out to all 4 teams asynchronously, no impact on the production app's performance. Transactions (A) don't notify external systems. Direct SNS publish from the app (B) tightly couples the app to notifications. Cron-based scanning (D) is high overhead and scales poorly. Mental shortcut: 'react to DynamoDB inserts without affecting app + notify multiple teams' = DynamoDB Streams + Lambda + SNS fan-out.
tricks: 'react to DynamoDB inserts without affecting app + notify multiple teams' = DynamoDB Streams + Lambda + SNS fan-out

cards.q: A company wants to use the AWS Cloud to make an existing application highly available and resilient. The current version of the application resides in the company's data center. The application recently experienced data loss after a database server crashed because of an unexpected power outage. The company needs a solution that avoids any single points of failure. The solution must give the application the ability to scale to meet user demand. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: A. Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ configuration.
options: Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ configuration.
Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group in a single Availability Zone. Deploy the database on an EC2 instance. Enable EC2 Auto Recovery.

Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon RDS DB instance with a read replica in a single Availability Zone. Promote the read replica to replace the primary DB instance if the primary DB instance fails.

Deploy the application servers by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Deploy the primary and secondary database servers on EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach to create shared storage between the instances.
cards.explanation: EC2 ASG across multiple AZs + RDS Multi-AZ removes single points of failure at every tier and supports scaling. Single-AZ ASG with EC2 DB (B) keeps the SPOF. Read replica in single AZ (C) doesn't auto-promote and the AZ failure still impacts. EBS Multi-Attach for shared DB storage (D) is not a database HA pattern. Mental shortcut: 'no single point of failure + scalable' = ASG multi-AZ + RDS Multi-AZ.
tricks: 'no single point of failure + scalable' = ASG multi-AZ + RDS Multi-AZ

cards.q: A company needs to ingest and handle large amounts of streaming data that its application generates. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances and sends data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, which is configured with default settings. Every other day, the application consumes the data and writes the data to an Amazon S3 bucket for business intelligence (BI) processing. The company observes that Amazon S3 is not receiving all the data that the application sends to Kinesis Data Streams. What should a solutions architect do to resolve this issue?
cards.a: A. Update the Kinesis Data Streams default settings by modifying the data retention period.
options: Update the Kinesis Data Streams default settings by modifying the data retention period.
Update the application to use the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) to send the data to Kinesis Data Streams.
Update the number of Kinesis shards to handle the throughput of the data that is sent to Kinesis Data Streams.
Turn on S3 Versioning within the S3 bucket to preserve every version of every object that is ingested in the S3 bucket.
cards.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams default retention is 24 hours, but the consumer runs only every 48 hours, so records expire before they are read. Increasing the data retention period (A) fixes the loss. Adding shards (C) addresses throughput, not retention. ExamTopics consensus: A.
tricks: 'Kinesis throughput limits' = increase shards

cards.q: A developer has an application that uses an AWS Lambda function to upload files to Amazon S3 and needs the required permissions to perform the task. The developer already has an IAM user with valid IAM credentials required for Amazon S3. What should a solutions architect do to grant the permissions?
cards.a: D. Create an IAM execution role with the required permissions and attach the IAM role to the Lambda function.
options: Add required IAM permissions in the resource policy of the Lambda function.
Create a signed request using the existing IAM credentials in the Lambda function.
Create a new IAM user and use the existing IAM credentials in the Lambda function.
Create an IAM execution role with the required permissions and attach the IAM role to the Lambda function.
cards.explanation: Lambda execution roles are the standard way to grant a Lambda function permissions to call AWS APIs (S3 PutObject here). Resource policies (A) on Lambda control who can invoke the function, not what the function can do. Reusing IAM user credentials (B, C) violates least privilege and bakes credentials into code. Mental shortcut: 'Lambda needs to access an AWS service' = IAM execution role attached to the function.
tricks: 'Lambda needs to access an AWS service' = IAM execution role attached to the function

cards.q: A company has deployed a serverless application that invokes an AWS Lambda function when new documents are uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket. The application uses the Lambda function to process the documents. After a recent marketing campaign, the company noticed that the application did not process many of the documents. What should a solutions architect do to improve the architecture of this application?
cards.a: D. Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Send the requests to the queue. Configure the queue as an event source for Lambda.
options: Set the Lambda function's runtime timeout value to 15 minutes.
Configure an S3 bucket replication policy. Stage the documents in the S3 bucket for later processing.
Deploy an additional Lambda function. Load balance the processing of the documents across the two Lambda functions.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Send the requests to the queue. Configure the queue as an event source for Lambda.
cards.explanation: If S3 events directly trigger Lambda and the burst exceeds Lambda concurrency, events are dropped. Inserting an SQS queue between S3 and Lambda buffers the events (durability, retries, DLQ) so no event is lost during marketing campaigns. Longer Lambda timeout (A) doesn't fix dropped events. CRR (B) just copies, doesn't queue. Two Lambdas without buffering (C) doesn't solve the burst problem. Mental shortcut: 'Lambda dropping events during bursts' = put SQS in front, set Lambda event source to SQS.
tricks: 'Lambda dropping events during bursts' = put SQS in front, set Lambda event source to SQS

cards.q: A solutions architect is designing the architecture for a software demonstration environment. The environment will run on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The system will experience significant increases in traffic during working hours but is not required to operate on weekends. Which combination of actions should the solutions architect take to ensure that the system can scale to meet demand? (Choose two.)
cards.a: D. Use a target tracking scaling policy to scale the Auto Scaling group based on instance CPU utilization. ; E. Use scheduled scaling to change the Auto Scaling group minimum, maximum, and desired capacity to zero for weekends. Revert to the default values at the start of the week.
options: Use AWS Auto Scaling to adjust the ALB capacity based on request rate.
Use AWS Auto Scaling to scale the capacity of the VPC internet gateway.
Launch the EC2 instances in multiple AWS Regions to distribute the load across Regions.
Use a target tracking scaling policy to scale the Auto Scaling group based on instance CPU utilization.
Use scheduled scaling to change the Auto Scaling group minimum, maximum, and desired capacity to zero for weekends. Revert to the default values at the start of the week.
cards.explanation: Target tracking on CPU (D) auto-scales during working hours based on actual load. Scheduled scaling to capacity zero on weekends (E) saves money when the app isn't needed. ALB doesn't need to be scaled (A) (it auto-scales). Internet gateway is not scalable (B). Multi-Region (C) is not for capacity, it's for global reach. Mental shortcut: 'scale up on demand + zero on weekends' = target tracking + scheduled scaling.
tricks: 'scale up on demand + zero on weekends' = target tracking + scheduled scaling

cards.q: A solutions architect is designing a two-tiered architecture that includes a public subnet and a database subnet. The web servers in the public subnet must be open to the internet on port 443. The Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the database subnet must be accessible only to the web servers on port 3306. Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
cards.a: C. Create a security group for the web servers in the public subnet. Add a rule to allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443. ; D. Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.
options: Create a network ACL for the public subnet. Add a rule to deny outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 3306.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the public subnet CIDR block on port 3306.
Create a security group for the web servers in the public subnet. Add a rule to allow traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to allow traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.
Create a security group for the DB instance. Add a rule to deny all traffic except traffic from the web servers’ security group on port 3306.
cards.explanation: Two-tier least privilege: web SG allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (C), DB SG allows 3306 only from the web SG (D). Using CIDR blocks for tier-to-tier (B) leaks too much. NACLs are stateless and not the right primary control here (A). 'Deny all except from web SG' (E) is implicit because SG default deny applies; explicit deny rules don't exist in SGs. Mental shortcut: 'two-tier least privilege' = SG referencing the upstream SG.
tricks: 'two-tier least privilege' = SG referencing the upstream SG

cards.q: A company is implementing a shared storage solution for a gaming application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs the ability to use Lustre clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed. Which solution meets these requirements?
cards.a: D. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
options: Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.
Create an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway. Create a file share that uses the required client protocol. Connect the application server to the file share.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and configure it to support Lustre. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
cards.explanation: Amazon FSx for Lustre is the fully managed Lustre service for high-performance shared file systems used in HPC, ML, and gaming workloads. EFS (C) is NFS POSIX, doesn't speak Lustre. Storage Gateway (B) is for hybrid file access. DataSync (A) is a transfer service. Mental shortcut: 'Lustre + fully managed' = Amazon FSx for Lustre.
tricks: 'Lustre + fully managed' = Amazon FSx for Lustre
'HPC + sub-millisecond + S3 link' = FSx for Lustre

cards.q: A company runs an application that receives data from thousands of geographically dispersed remote devices that use UDP. The application processes the data immediately and sends a message back to the device if necessary. No data is stored. The company needs a solution that minimizes latency for the data transmission from the devices. The solution also must provide rapid failover to another AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: B. Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the NLProcess the data in Amazon ECS.
options: Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions. Configure the NLB to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the data.

Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the NLProcess the data in Amazon ECS.

Use AWS Global Accelerator. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions as an endpoint. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.

Configure an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each of the two Regions. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Fargate launch type. Create an ECS service on the cluster. Set the ECS service as the target for the ALB. Process the data in Amazon ECS.
cards.explanation: Global Accelerator with NLB endpoints provides static anycast IPs and sub-second cross-Region failover for any TCP/UDP traffic (the question implies binary protocol via NLB). NLB is layer 4. ECS Fargate scales the data processing. ALB (C) is HTTP-only. Route 53 failover (D) has DNS-cache-bound recovery (minutes). Lambda+EventBridge (A) is a different processing pattern. Mental shortcut: 'multi-Region + low-latency failover + binary/TCP protocol' = Global Accelerator + NLB + ECS Fargate.
tricks: 'multi-Region + low-latency failover + binary/TCP protocol' = Global Accelerator + NLB + ECS Fargate
'UDP traffic' = NLB only (ALB does NOT support UDP); for global VoIP add Global Accelerator

cards.q: A solutions architect must migrate a Windows Internet Information Services (IIS) web application to AWS. The application currently relies on a file share hosted in the user's on-premises network-attached storage (NAS). The solutions architect has proposed migrating the IIS web servers to Amazon EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones that are connected to the storage solution, and configuring an Elastic Load Balancer attached to the instances. Which replacement to the on-premises file share is MOST resilient and durable?
cards.a: C. Migrate the file share to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
options: Migrate the file share to Amazon RDS.
Migrate the file share to AWS Storage Gateway.
Migrate the file share to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
Migrate the file share to Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).
cards.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed SMB file system with multi-AZ resilience and NTFS ACLs, ideal as a drop-in for IIS apps that read NAS-style file shares. RDS (A) is a database. Storage Gateway (B) is for hybrid scenarios. EFS (D) is NFS Linux, not native to IIS/Windows. Mental shortcut: 'IIS Windows file share + multi-AZ' = Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
tricks: 'IIS Windows file share + multi-AZ' = Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

cards.q: A company is deploying a new application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application writes data to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The company needs to ensure that all data that is written to the EBS volumes is encrypted at rest. Which solution will meet this requirement?
cards.a: B. Create the EBS volumes as encrypted volumes. Attach the EBS volumes to the EC2 instances.
options: Create an IAM role that specifies EBS encryption. Attach the role to the EC2 instances.
Create the EBS volumes as encrypted volumes. Attach the EBS volumes to the EC2 instances.
Create an EC2 instance tag that has a key of Encrypt and a value of True. Tag all instances that require encryption at the EBS level.
Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key policy that enforces EBS encryption in the account. Ensure that the key policy is active.
cards.explanation: EBS encryption is enabled at volume creation time using a KMS key (or default). Existing volumes can't be encrypted in place; you must create encrypted volumes (or snapshot+copy with encryption). IAM role for encryption (A) doesn't exist. Tags (C) don't enforce encryption. KMS key policy (D) governs key access, not whether volumes are encrypted. Mental shortcut: 'ensure EBS data is encrypted at rest' = create the volumes as encrypted.
tricks: 'ensure EBS data is encrypted at rest' = create the volumes as encrypted

cards.q: A company has a web application with sporadic usage patterns. There is heavy usage at the beginning of each month, moderate usage at the start of each week, and unpredictable usage during the week. The application consists of a web server and a MySQL database server running inside the data center. The company would like to move the application to the AWS Cloud, and needs to select a cost-effective database platform that will not require database modifications. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: C. MySQL-compatible Amazon Aurora Serverless
options: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon RDS for MySQL
MySQL-compatible Amazon Aurora Serverless
MySQL deployed on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group
cards.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 (MySQL-compatible) auto-scales capacity in seconds based on demand, perfect for sporadic/unpredictable usage, and no app changes are needed (drop-in MySQL). RDS for MySQL (B) requires manual or scheduled scaling. DynamoDB (A) is NoSQL, requires DB rewrite. EC2 ASG with MySQL (D) is high overhead. Mental shortcut: 'sporadic MySQL + auto-scale + no app change' = Aurora Serverless MySQL-compatible.
tricks: 'sporadic MySQL + auto-scale + no app change' = Aurora Serverless MySQL-compatible

cards.q: An image-hosting company stores its objects in Amazon S3 buckets. The company wants to avoid accidental exposure of the objects in the S3 buckets to the public. All S3 objects in the entire AWS account need to remain private. Which solution will meet these requirements?
cards.a: D. Use the S3 Block Public Access feature on the account level. Use AWS Organizations to create a service control policy (SCP) that prevents IAM users from changing the setting. Apply the SCP to the account.
options: Use Amazon GuardDuty to monitor S3 bucket policies. Create an automatic remediation action rule that uses an AWS Lambda function to remediate any change that makes the objects public.

Use AWS Trusted Advisor to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Configure email notifications in Trusted Advisor when a change is detected. Manually change the S3 bucket policy if it allows public access.

Use AWS Resource Access Manager to find publicly accessible S3 buckets. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a change is detected. Deploy a Lambda function that programmatically remediates the change.

Use the S3 Block Public Access feature on the account level. Use AWS Organizations to create a service control policy (SCP) that prevents IAM users from changing the setting. Apply the SCP to the account.
cards.explanation: S3 Block Public Access (BPA) at the account level prevents any S3 bucket in the account from being made public, regardless of bucket policy or ACL.
